title: Social Media Monitoring
thesis: Examines Indian government social media monitoring programs, arguing they lack legal basis, transparency, and accountability, threatening privacy and free speech.
key_quotes: Social media monitoring techniques have their origins in the private sector. These practices were, to begin with, aimed at market research and customer profiling. With time, law enforcement agencies have recognised their utility. || The use of machine learning algorithms and big data multiply these harms by reducing the transparency and intelligibility of these decisions. || In absence of any laws which govern the functioning of these applications, there is no way to ensure that basic human rights such as free speech, privacy and the right to assemble and protest are not curtailed.
policy_relevance: Argues for clear legal framework, transparency, accountability, and judicial oversight for social media surveillance programs. Critiques lack of legislation and mission creep.

title: NITI Aayog Discussion Paper: An aspirational step towards India’s AI policy
thesis: Critique of India's AI strategy for insufficient attention to ethics, rights, defense dual-use, and over-reliance on industry self-regulation.
key_quotes: Another sector the paper fails to include is defense, this is worrying since India is chairing the Group of Governmental Experts on Lethal Autonomous Weapons Systems (LAWS) in 2018. || In its vision for the use of AI in smart cities, the paper suggests the adoption of a sophisticated surveillance system as well as the use of social media intelligence platforms to check and monitor people’s movement both online and offline to maintain public safety. || The section on transparency and opening the Black Box has several lacunae.
policy_relevance: Recommends future AI strategy include defense applications, human rights impact assessments, mandatory human-in-the-loop, kill switches, and stronger regulatory frameworks; criticises over-reliance on industry self-regulation.

title: Big Brother Watch’s written evidence to the Joint Committee on Human Rights on The Right to Privacy (Article 8) and the Digital Revolution inquiry
thesis: State adoption of surveillance technologies and automated decision-making in policing and welfare systems threatens privacy rights, requiring stronger legal safeguards.
key_quotes: Police are also using more and more advanced technology to access, download, and analyse digital evidence as part of these investigations. However, technological and legal and policy limitations currently mean that digital evidence collection can be extremely intrusive, obstruct justice, and infringe rights. || The public sector is rapidly adopting commercial software, either replacing human functions or introducing new processes. This includes machine-learning, predictive policing systems; artificial intelligence (AI) facial recognition surveillance software; AI recidivism risk tools fuelled by marketing data; automated risk assessments and ‘Voice Risk Analysis’ for welfare applicants; and digital evidence software, including AI analysis, in the criminal justice system. || The UK’s Data Protection Act 2018 makes exemptions from this important GDPR right. ... welfare and justice decisions could be being made that are for all intents and purposes automated decisions, without individuals being notified of this fact or of their right to appeal.
policy_relevance: Recommends formal public and parliamentary consultations before adoption of new technologies, amendments to Data Protection Act 2018 to ban fully automated decisions engaging human rights, and banning micro-targeted online advertising. Also recommends a public inventory of public-private data sharing agreements.

title: Public Comment
thesis: A public comment letter expressing concern that Smart City technologies in Tracy constitute mass surveillance and encroach on privacy, free speech, and data protection.
key_quotes: Smart Cities are not being accurately described for what they really are - they are mass surveillance cities, which remove any sense of individual privacy. || The deployment and integration of surveillance technologies, such as sensors and biometric data collection systems - electronic, infrared, thermal, and LIDAR sensors form the basis of the smart grid. They do everything from operating streetlights to optimizing parking and traffic flow to detect crime. || nobody would vote for digital prisons if they understood how vast the surveillance will be in smart cities.
policy_relevance: The comment requests the city council to reevaluate the Smart City plan and consider privacy implications, but offers no specific policy recommendations.

title: Future Cities: Trends and Implications
thesis: The report identifies trends in future cities and their military implications for UK defence operations.
key_quotes: The exploitation of smart technology may permit the ability to map occurrences within a building in real-time; allowing effective collateral damage estimations, to better inform the most suitable form of kinetic strike. || Smart City infrastructure poses risks and opportunities for the UK military. If an adversary is able to efficiently control digital infrastructure and deny the UK military access, they will be able to utilise it to gain an advantage. || The increasing verticalisation of buildings, and urban density, will make it difficult to contain weapon effects within a single building or floor, enhancing the likelihood of collateral damage.
policy_relevance: Provides recommendations for UK military: urban training, database of cities, specialised urban units, cyber capabilities, and partnerships with private sector.

title: Open letter to EU AI Act negotiators: Do not trade away our rights!
thesis: Civil society calls on EU lawmakers to reject legalisation of dangerous and discriminatory police AI in the AI Act.
key_quotes: No AI Act deal can be worth legitimising digital tools of oppression. || EU Member States are pushing extremist demands for police to be able to discriminate against the general public including on the basis of race, gender, sexuality, religion and political views through predictive policing and biometric categorisation systems. || These technologies are rooted in eugenic, racist and ableist premises, and have been widely discredited by academics.
policy_relevance: Direct advocacy for the EU AI Act to prohibit predictive policing, biometric categorisation, emotion recognition, and mass surveillance in policing and migration, and to ensure transparency and accountability.

title: COMMENTS OF THE ELECTRONIC PRIVACY INFORMATION CENTER to the U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security Request for Written Submissions on Section 13(e) of EO 14074
thesis: EPIC argues that law enforcement use of facial recognition, predictive algorithms, social media surveillance, and DNA analysis requires robust safeguards to protect privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties, and that some technologies should be banned.
key_quotes: By enabling surveillance at scale and at minimum cost, these emerging surveillance tools allow law enforcement to quickly identify and track individuals to an extent previously impossible. Given this scalability and the current lack of safeguards, the risk of mission creep is significant. || Facial recognition is a dangerous and privacy-invasive surveillance technology that law enforcement should not use. ... It is a perfect tool of oppression and poses far too great a risk to our democracy to become a ubiquitous tool of police surveillance. || Predictive technology trained on historical policing data reinforces the over policing of majority minority neighborhoods and communities, while dehumanizing those communities and adding a veneer of legitimacy and objectivity through 'hard data.'
policy_relevance: The document provides ten detailed policy recommendations for DOJ and DHS, including prohibiting mass surveillance, requiring warrants, mandating independent audits, strengthening data minimization, and ensuring non-discrimination. It also calls for a ban on facial recognition technology and stricter regulation of predictive policing, social media surveillance, and DNA databases.

title: INFORMATION, KNOWLEDGE AND DIGITAL DISRUPTION
thesis: Symposium exploring how emerging digital technologies will disrupt Defence and national security in smart city contexts over 10-20 years.
key_quotes: In the next 10 to 20 years, new technologies such as the internet of things, big data, artificial intelligence, machine learning, robotics, automation and virtual/augmented/mixed reality will transform the way we live our lives. In the Defence context this rapid change (resulting in disruption) presents both an opportunity and a threat. || How will our future organisational and command structures operate with the agility and flexibility offered by digital technologies? And equally, how will our adversaries adopt and use such technologies. || Cities in 2040 will be hyper-connected information nodes in the digital mesh, and how Defence interacts with this environment is an important insight for forward strategic planning.
policy_relevance: Symposium aims to shape long-term Defence and national security research priorities and industry focus through a Big Picture Assessment Report.

title: Big Data Applications in Crime and Security
SMART CITY TECHNOLOGIES. SMART BASE NEEDS.
geography: United States (Fort Carson, Fort Benning, MCAS Miramar)
thesis: Promotes dual-use development of commercial smart city technologies for military installations to enhance readiness and resilience.
key_quotes: US Ignite and our partners promote the rapid dual-use development of commercial technologies that meet the needs of installations. || Just like cities, Department of Defense (DoD) installations are tasked with taking care of their people, promoting readiness and resilience, and delivering critical services to residents and visitors. This overlap means military installations can take advantage of existing smart city solutions to modernize operations and create their own more effective Smart Base operations. || If a piloted solution is successful, US Ignite and our partners then communicate the success of the program and work to identify pathways for entrenching the technology in the host installation and scaling it to installations across the DoD.
policy_relevance: Promotes a model for dual-use technology development and scaling across military installations, with implications for defense procurement and smart city-military collaboration.

title: Huawei's Smart Cities and CCP Influence, At Home and Abroad
thesis: Huawei's smart city technologies, while commercially marketed, can be leveraged by the CCP for surveillance and social control at home and potentially extend authoritarian influence abroad.
key_quotes: Huawei compares its flagship smart city product, its 'Intelligent Operation Center', to a smart city ‘brain’ that guides and makes sense of the input from the city’s ‘nervous system’—networked cameras and other sensing devices— to provide comprehensible, actionable information on crime and unrest to police and municipal decisionmakers. || Whether Huawei’s safe city technologies are being employed by authoritarian and kleptocratic regimes to reinforce their rule is an understudied question. However, it is both interesting and suggestive that the list of countries where Huawei’s safe city solutions were first deployed includes a number of authoritarian and hybrid regimes with close ties to China, among them Russia, Pakistan, Venezuela, Laos, and Angola. || While the smart cities of the future could be better, more efficient cities, they could also provide authoritarian regimes with previously undreamt of tools of surveillance and control.
policy_relevance: Raises concerns about foreign intelligence risks from Huawei equipment in Western municipalities, and suggests need for caution in adopting smart city technologies from companies with ties to authoritarian regimes.

title: Smart Cities with Chinese Characteristics
thesis: Chinese smart city systems exported globally pose dual-use risks to national security and privacy, requiring comprehensive national planning in Israel.
key_quotes: Autocratic regimes can effectively exploit these technologies to reinforce their power and tighten control over their populations. || Chinese companies export various smart city systems to dozens of countries, including Israel, notwithstanding Western allegations of breaches of human rights and dangers to national security. || The social credit rating is one aspect of the Communist Party's efforts to use advanced technology in order to monitor the public and reinforce its control, for the benefit of what it perceives as protection of national security and internal stability.
policy_relevance: Recommends Israel prepare a comprehensive national plan to map existing situation, identify challenges, manage risks to privacy, data security, and cyber protection, and review foreign relations of local authorities regarding smart tech.

title: U.S.-China Competition in Emerging Technologies: LiDAR
thesis: LiDAR is a dual-use technology with both civilian and military applications, and U.S.-China competition in LiDAR poses national security risks due to Chinese industrial policies and technology transfer.
key_quotes: Some emerging technologies have both civilian and military uses. Among these technologies is Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR), a remote sensing technology used in automotive, agriculture, weather, manufacturing, and other systems. || The United States first developed LiDAR as a military technology in the 1960s for defense and aerospace uses. Since then, the LiDAR market has expanded with the development of systems capable of autonomous navigation, for which LiDAR is a critical enabling technology. || PRC policies seek to develop technologies that are interoperable for civilian and military use and may allow PRC state access.
policy_relevance: Discusses issues for Congress: strengthening procurement rules to review/restrict acquisition of PRC LiDAR, economic tools related to foreign investment, export controls, fair trade, antitrust, standards, capital markets, IP licensing, and bankruptcy.

title: China's smart cities and the future of geopolitics
geography: China, Malaysia, Kenya, Pakistan, Uganda, Mauritius, Philippines, Papua New Guinea, Indonesia, India, France, Germany
thesis: Chinese smart city and city brain technologies, driven by civil-military fusion, are geostrategic tools that enable surveillance, military integration, and global influence.
key_quotes: The Institute—which focuses on eclectic subjects like intelligent wargaming, swarm intelligence, aerospace security and the city brain—explains the urban brain's value for the military brain: 'It can be said that the confrontation of wars between countries in the future will be reflected in … [confrontations] between several military brains. Based on the research progress of the urban brain, we can combine various military elements into a brain-like combination to form the structural diagram of the military brain[.]' || Smart city systems are highly complex, which makes it difficult for importing countries to scrutinise them. City brains—the next evolutionary step of smart cities—are even more complex, potentially incomprehensible, because of their extensive deployment of artificial intelligence. Little appears to be done to increase the auditability of those system. || The smarter its exported surveillance infrastructure becomes; the easier spying becomes. ... the smarter its exported surveillance infrastructure, the more influence it can wield in those regions, since it has a privileged but not exclusive capability to control its technology within a given territory.
policy_relevance: Recommends that democracies draw up initiatives promoting privacy-friendly smart urban turnkey solutions that can compete globally, and expand research on privacy-enhancing technologies for law enforcement.

title: AI Global Surveillance (AIGS) Index
thesis: This index maps the global adoption of AI-based surveillance technologies, linking them to regime characteristics and military spending.
key_quotes: AI Global Surveillance (AIGS) Index || Aggregate Regime Score: Comprised of evenly weighted average of country scores from Freedom in the World 2019, the EIU Democracy Index 2018, and the V-Dem Dataset version 9, Electoral Democracy Index. || Countries with an average score less than 2.5 are labeled closed autocracies.
policy_relevance: Provides data on global surveillance technology adoption, useful for policy analysis on the relationship between regime type and surveillance infrastructure.

title: WE SENSE TROUBLE: AUTOMATED DISCRIMINATION AND MASS SURVEILLANCE IN PREDICTIVE POLICING IN THE NETHERLANDS
thesis: The Dutch police's Sensing project in Roermond constitutes unlawful mass surveillance and discrimination through predictive policing, violating privacy, data protection, and non-discrimination rights.
key_quotes: The Sensing project includes indiscriminate mass surveillance because it monitors behaviour by tracking movement which is not targeted at a very specific location (an entire city), nor at specific individuals or groups, and it is not based on reasonable suspicion; the data of all people travelling by car is collected and analysed. || The police present the predictive policing system as a neutral system, guided by objective criminal data statistics, while in reality the Sensing project embodies human choices and biased data, which results in amplifying and entrenching bias in policing. || The use of the concept of ‘mobile banditry’ inevitably leads to a predominant focus on particular groups of people on the grounds of their nationality and ethnicity, while at the same time overlooking people from other ethnic and/or national backgrounds.
policy_relevance: The report provides detailed recommendations to Dutch law enforcement, legislature, and data protection authority, including halting the Sensing project, prohibiting algorithmic systems without safeguards, implementing mandatory human rights impact assessments, and creating an independent supervisory authority.

title: COMMENTS OF THE ELECTRONIC PRIVACY INFORMATION CENTER to the U.S. Department of Justice and Department of Homeland Security Request for Written Submissions on Section 13(e) of EO 14074
thesis: Law enforcement use of surveillance technologies like facial recognition, predictive algorithms, social media monitoring, and DNA analysis poses severe risks to civil rights and liberties, requiring a framework of ten protective principles.
key_quotes: Facial recognition is a dangerous and privacy-invasive surveillance technology that law enforcement should not use. || Predictive policing technology is based on discriminatory policing patterns. ... Running the data through a series of math formulas and code does not substantively change the biased nature of the original data that determines the rules in the new algorithm. || The more a child engages with law enforcement, the more likely they are to enter the revolving door of the criminal justice system.
policy_relevance: The paper provides extensive recommendations for DOJ and DHS, including prohibiting mass surveillance, requiring warrants, independent audits, data minimization, and transparency. It calls for enforceable safeguards to protect civil rights and civil liberties.

title: Paradigm Initiative’s input to the OHCHR, to inform the Special Rapporteur’s 2025 Position Paper on the Human Rights Impacts of Using Artificial Intelligence in Countering Terrorism, including guidance on good practices.
thesis: AI in counter-terrorism poses significant human rights risks, particularly through surveillance, predictive policing, and dual-use technologies, and requires robust safeguards and oversight.
key_quotes: In Ghana, governments often monitor journalists and political opponents using military-grade spyware such as Pegasus. African governments frequently justify these highly intrusive actions as efforts to combat terrorism and protect national security. || The 'black box' nature of many AI systems, where the logic behind decisions is not easily explainable, undermines transparency and complicates oversight across borders. || Unregulated sale and transfer of AI tools for counter-terrorism, such as predictive analytics or facial recognition, can facilitate repression and human rights violations.
policy_relevance: Recommends embedding human rights safeguards in the AI lifecycle, including impact assessments, transparency, accountability, and oversight mechanisms; references the EU Dual-Use Regulation, Council of Europe Framework Convention, and UNICRI-INTERPOL Toolkit as normative instruments.

title: China's Digital Silk Road
geography: global (focus on Asia, China, US, Japan)
thesis: Panel discussion on China's Digital Silk Road examining strategic, economic, and security implications for US-Japan cooperation.
key_quotes: China's BDS navigation system is problematic, particularly when China's already demonstrated a willingness to militarize space. The sensors, the enhanced guidance, the dual use of this, in addition to everything it's doing in the cyber domain is problematic.
policy_relevance: Calls for US-Japan public-private partnership to compete with China's Digital Silk Road, including strengthening risk financing, international rulemaking on data flows, and capacity-building in emerging Asia.

title: The Rise of Chinese AI in the Gulf: a Renewal of China's 'Serbia Model'
thesis: China uses a 'Serbia model' of technology transfer from civilian AI/smart city systems to military cooperation to expand influence in the Gulf.
key_quotes: Beijing is using a model it pioneered in Serbia to expand its technological and military interests in the Persian Gulf. || China is using lessons it learned interacting with Serbia to improve its approach toward the Middle East by first building up basic infrastructure, then adding on technology systems, and finally launching bilateral military cooperation. || Huawei has strategically marketed its Safe City technology to Saudi Arabia as an advanced, streamlined way to counter extremism and enhance urban safety.
policy_relevance: Recommends US counter China by diversifying tech suppliers, ensuring data security, and offering higher quality products; also suggests loosening arms export restrictions.

title: BRIEF OF AMICUS CURIAE ELECTRONIC PRIVACY INFORMATION CENTER (EPIC) IN SUPPORT OF PLAINTIFFS-APPELLANTS AND URGING REVERSAL
thesis: Argues that warrantless use of modern ALPR systems violates the Fourth Amendment because they reveal privacies of life and enable discriminatory predictive policing.
key_quotes: Modern ALPR systems not only amass vast troves of sensitive location information but also knit it together with other information—commercial and otherwise—that allows law enforcement to infer identity and monitor the habits and routines of everyday people. || The decisions made by an ALPR system are cloaked in objectivity and hidden in a proprietary black box, making it nearly impossible for someone to fully vindicate their rights under the Fourth and Fifth Amendments. || AI-enabled ALPRs likewise facilitate abuses of power akin to the general warrant... applied broadly to entire populations, enabling the state to both generate suspicion and marshal evidence post hoc.
policy_relevance: Argues for warrant requirement for ALPR systems, increased transparency, and accountability to prevent abuse and discriminatory policing.

title: EU's AI Act fails to set gold standard for human rights
thesis: The EU AI Act fails to adequately protect human rights, with loopholes for law enforcement and migration, and allows export of harmful AI systems.
key_quotes: The AI Act does not stop EU-based companies from exporting AI systems which are banned in the EU, therefore creating a huge risk of violating rights of people in non-EU countries by EU-made technologies that are essentially incompatible with human rights. || The major shortcoming of the EU database is that negotiators agreed on a carve-out for law enforcement, migration, asylum and border control authorities. Providers and deployers of high-risk systems in these areas will be requested to register only a limited amount of information, and only in a non-publicly accessible section of the database. || The blanket exemption for national security risks undermining other rules: The AI Act and its safeguards will not apply to AI systems if they are developed or used solely for the purpose of national security, and regardless of whether this is done by a public authority or a private company.
policy_relevance: The paper recommends comprehensive bans on unacceptable AI uses, meaningful transparency and stakeholder engagement, no national security exemption, and extension of human rights safeguards to exported AI systems. It calls for civil society inclusion in implementation.

title: POLICIAMENTO PREDITIVO EM FORTALEZA: SEGURANÇA PÚBLICA E O USO DE FERRAMENTAS TECNOLÓGICAS NA PREVENÇÃO DO CRIME
thesis: Proposes implementing predictive policing software in Fortaleza to prevent homicides using historical crime data for efficient police resource allocation.
key_quotes: A ideia central é que, em vez de aumentar o efetivo policial, ou quando ele é reduzido, empregar melhor os policiais a serviço nas áreas onde se sabe que o crime pode ocorrer. Por meio de um algoritmo (sistema que mostra passo a passo os procedimentos necessários para a resolução de uma tarefa) que, alimentado de uma imensa quantidade de dados, poderá prever crimes antes que aconteçam. || O policiamento preditivo é um processo de policiamento ostensivo, com características preventivas diferenciadas, que trabalha com previsões testáveis, ou seja, previsões baseadas em históricos de crimes em determinada área, especialmente em quadrantes de bairros com maior incidência delitiva e que causam maior sensação de insegurança à população. || É possível que, conforme a sociedade adquira confiança na previsão dos sistemas, os moradores de um bairro X onde o algoritmo indique maior probabilidade de crime, acabem passando por ações sem que nem moradores nem os policiais saibam bem o motivo.
policy_relevance: The paper proposes a detailed intervention plan for implementing predictive policing in Fortaleza, including strategies, resource allocation, training, and a timeline. It suggests collaboration with SSPDS, SUPESP, and AESP, and emphasizes the need for well-trained police to use the technology effectively.

title: Privacy Challenges and Big Data in Smart City
thesis: The paper examines privacy challenges in Hong Kong's smart city initiatives, highlighting gaps between existing governance, public trust, and socio-political contexts through case studies of smart lampposts and facial recognition.
key_quotes: The public concern focuses on whether smart lampposts will become a surveillance system similar to mainland China's, conducting facial recognition on everyone on the street, becoming a tool for police and government to suppress protesters. || The new forms of personal data and privacy are deeply embedded in socio-political relations. This boundary between the public and the private domains could not be defined simply in technical and legal terms. || The foremost task is to regain the public's confidence... the government should make a public statement to promise not to implement some politically sensitive technologies, such as automated or random facial recognition.
policy_relevance: Recommends rebuilding public trust, enacting a Protection of Freedoms Act-like ordinance, mandating Privacy Impact Assessments (PIA) for government, requiring data flow charts, and establishing an independent body to monitor national security-related data collection.

title: Sinergia ‒ condiție esențială a succesului în procesul planificării civil-militare în orașul inteligent / Synergy ‒ the essential condition of success in the civil-military planning process of the smart city
thesis: Civil-military synergy and data sharing are essential for efficient smart city governance and security across peace, crisis, and war.
key_quotes: Asigurarea securității multidimensionale (sociale, de mediu, de servicii, cibernetice etc.) în orașele inteligente contribuie în mod semnificativ la reducerea cheltuielilor de funcționare a serviciilor publice, alături de reducerea timpului consumat de utilizatori pentru accesul la aceste servicii, participând, astfel, la creșterea nivelului de trai al populației. || Pentru asigurarea securității cetățenilor și a infrastructurilor critice, este necesară cooperarea civil-militară continuă, care să asigure funcționarea eficientă a orașelor la pace, în situații de criză sau la război. || Astfel, sinergia este o condiție esențială pentru asigurarea funcționării eficiente a orașului inteligent, la pace, în situații de criză sau la război.
policy_relevance: Recommends integrated civil-military spatial planning, continuous monitoring, and data-sharing platforms for smart city security, with emphasis on legal frameworks and citizen privacy.

title: Who buys and controls the CCTV? Myanmar's slippery slope to mass surveillance
thesis: CCTV infrastructure procured for civilian smart city projects in Myanmar has been repurposed by the military junta for mass surveillance and suppression of dissent, highlighting the urgent need for transparency and human rights safeguards.
key_quotes: CCTV cameras form the infrastructural backbone of a host of emerging technologies – including AI applications like facial and emotion recognition. The mission creep embedded in technical and policy design for CCTVs go from simply being installed cameras for ‘safety’, to being equipped to carry out remote biometric identification. || Overarchingly, we point to how opacity is normalised as a feature and not a bug within Myanmar’s technology procurement framework and we provide recommendations for a way forward. || In Myanmar, particularly since the coup, CCTV cameras have become a kind of weapon that repressive forces have seized and are using to silence dissent.
policy_relevance: The report provides detailed recommendations to the military junta (stop purchasing repressive technologies, restore democracy) and to the private sector (refrain from selling to authoritarian regimes, conduct human rights impact assessments). It also calls for a moratorium on procurement, data protection legislation, and a right to information law.

title: China’s Smart Cities Development
thesis: China's smart city initiatives are state-led, dual-use technologies enabling mass surveillance domestically and exported globally, posing economic and security challenges to the U.S.
key_quotes: China’s civilian informatization policies have been designed to account for national security interests and augment China’s military power whenever possible. China’s smart cities policies are not sui generis efforts and should not be taken as such; as the latest in a long series of 'urban informatization' policies, they exist as one component of a broader whole.
policy_relevance: The report offers multiple policy recommendations: create local task forces to track foreign smart city tech; support U.S. competitiveness internationally; engage in standard-setting bodies; prioritize Five Eyes and allied countries for vulnerability assessment; legislate supply chain protection for critical infrastructure.

title: Security in Modern Smart Cities: An Information Technology Perspective
thesis: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of security systems in smart cities, highlighting key trends, mass surveillance examples, and challenges for implementation.
key_quotes: 9/11 will be remembered as a watershed incident which made the world realize that the threat of mass terrorism is real and close. || Putting a surveillance camera on a roundabout would not stop any crime or terror activity by its own. What it sees, record and send to the command center must be analyzed as well if it has to contribute in a responsive security system for the city. || The security concepts highlighted in this article would help the network designers and system operators in formulating a flawless strategy for future smart cities.
policy_relevance: Discusses policy-level challenges including institutional disconnect, need for coordinated framework, governance, and financial strategies (private sector investment, phased implementation).

title: The Internet of Military Defense Things: A Smart City Assisted Internet of Military Defense Things Architecture
thesis: Proposes an architecture enabling future military forces to leverage Smart City IoT and deploy IoMDT for real-time situational awareness in intelligent urban environments.
key_quotes: the principle of leveraging existing Smart City infrastructure to enhance accurate and real-time Situational Awareness (SA) can be beneficial for future military operations || As Smart Cities become a reality, these intelligent urban environments will likely impact the future operational environment, where future military forces will have to conduct a range of operations. || we propose an architecture that enables future military forces, in a permissive intelligent urban operational environment, to access Smart City IoT, deploy their own IoMDT, and leverage distributed and opportunistic computing ... to produce and maintain accurate and real-time SA.
policy_relevance: None

title: Will GPS Jammers Proliferate in the Smart City?
thesis: The normalisation of tracking in the Smart City may lead to wider ownership of GPS jammers, requiring countermeasures and privacy safeguards.
key_quotes: Since the collapse of the Soviet Union, and when GPS became available for civilians in the 1990s, jamming and counter-jamming technologies have created new markets in the civilian realm and ceased to be confined exclusively to conflict zones and repressed states. || As GPS gets incorporated into civilian infrastructure and systems, animosities between adversaries in military conflicts and political animosities in the civilian domain fuse together. || The article offers possible counter-measures and alternative technologies, either built-in or as alternative navigation aids.
policy_relevance: The paper recommends stricter laws on privacy and jammer possession, granting more privacy to likely end-users (e.g., commercial drivers), and investing in alternative navigation systems (e.g., eLoran) to reduce GPS dependence.

title: Public Trust and Political Legitimacy in the Smart City: A Reckoning for Technocracy
thesis: Examines how public trust and political legitimacy affect support for smart city endeavors in Hong Kong using survey data, finding tensions between technocracy and democracy.
key_quotes: technocracy presents only an illusion of policymaking as 'sanitized' from politics. According to Hartley (2020), 'technocratic systems and policy design logics emerge from social and value-laden settings; neither materializes from a mythical purity of logic but is fashioned in politically and epistemically contested environments' (p. 237). || the smart city phenomenon invites critical reflection about tensions between technocracy and democracy, but this topic remains largely unexploited by empirical literature. || The implication is that the mechanics of smart cities have more legitimacy than the governance of smart cities.
policy_relevance: The study suggests that trust in technology and perceptions of democratic participation are important for public support of smart city programs, implying that governments should address privacy and participation concerns to enhance legitimacy.

title: Smart cities, backward frontiers: digital urbanism in India's north-east
thesis: India's Smart Cities Mission in the Northeast is a state-making project integrating frontier space into national territory, accelerating corporate capital entry, while local authorities use bids to request conventional infrastructure.
key_quotes: All ten smart city bids from the Northeast include reference to surveillance technology for things like traffic control, public transport management, and the 'safety and security' of citizens. In these cities the targets of safety and security campaigns have been local residents rather than generic criminals or miscreants. || The extension of the SCM to the Northeast is the latest in a long history of state-making projects – violent and non-violent – aimed at integrating frontier space into national territory, and in this case, 'backward' peoples into smart citizens. || Adding enhanced technology, facial recognition, and tracking data to this scenario is a frightening prospect for those deemed to be the beneficiaries of 'safety and security' measures, empowering and emboldening a brutal system of occupation.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the SCM's extension to sensitive spaces, highlighting risks of surveillance abuse, governance fragmentation, and the need to consider local customary authorities and military occupation in smart city planning. Recommends caution in implementing digital urbanism in militarized frontiers.

title: Application of IoT in Military Operations in a Smart City
thesis: This paper explores how smart city IoT infrastructure can be exploited for military operations to enhance situational awareness during disaster relief, addressing technical and security challenges.
key_quotes: This paper, which presents work performed by the NATO IST-147 'Military Applications of Internet of Things' group, explores the potential to exploit smart city IoT capabilities in military operations. || In a smart city environment with a significant deployment of Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, there is a potential to revolutionize SA by leveraging this new sensor capability. || The emergence of smart cities has led to the proliferation of such entities around cities either deployed by city authorities or by private individuals. The military may utilize the additional information of these sources in operations.
policy_relevance: None

title: A Survey of Applicability of Military Data Model Architectures for Smart City Data Consumption and Integration
thesis: Proposes an architectural concept to integrate Smart City data into military information systems using standardized military data models for improved situational awareness.
key_quotes: In these cases, an existing Smart City infrastructure can greatly assist emergency forces like relief units or supporting military forces by providing the data it already has. || This paper proposes an architectural concept for connecting to the Smart City data at different levels of aggregation. || The paper discusses how the available data and information from a Smart City infrastructure can be utilized to improve the SA of emergency forces like relief units or the military during an operation in a Smart City environment.
policy_relevance: None

title: Exploiting Smart City IoT for Disaster Recovery Operations
thesis: Proposes exploiting smart city IoT infrastructure to enhance situational awareness for disaster recovery operations, highlighting integration and security challenges.
key_quotes: In the event of a natural disaster phenomenon such as an earthquake, the IoT devices within the city such as the traffic cameras, weather, and pollution sensors can be re-tasked to identify emergency conditions such as toxic gases in the air, people trapped in vehicles or rubble, or the status of the power grid. || This paper envisions a HADR operation set in the near future after the advent of smart cities – where IoT technologies are widely deployed within a city infrastructure in order to improve the daily operations of the city... || Much of this work has been performed as part of a NATO Research Task Group (RTG) on Military Applications of Internet of Things (IST-147).
policy_relevance: Discusses security and integration challenges; recommends open standards, interoperability, and breaking-glass policies for emergency access to smart city data. Also suggests a priori federation of identity management.

title: A Survey of Applicability of Military Data Model Architectures for Smart City Data Consumption and Integration
thesis: Proposes an architectural concept and gateways to integrate Smart City data into military information systems using existing NATO data models.
key_quotes: In these cases, an existing Smart City infrastructure can greatly assist emergency forces like relief units or supporting military forces by providing the data it already has. || In case of missions within a Smart City environment, the available Smart City data could be used to improve the situational picture and thus contribute to a successful operation. || The paper discusses how the available data and information from a Smart City infrastructure can be utilized to improve the SA of emergency forces like relief units or the military during an operation in a Smart City environment.
policy_relevance: None directly, but implications for standardization and interoperability between civilian and military data systems.

title: Open Data Insights from a Smart Bridge Datathon: A Multi-Stakeholder Observation of Smart City Open Data in Practice
thesis: Open data from smart city infrastructure has nuanced benefits and risks, including power imbalances, potential for misuse, and challenges of transparency, as revealed by a datathon case study.
key_quotes: The last solo participant who joined late and also did not present was concerned about military, government, and corporations gaining access to the data—noting that open data also means open internationally. || Data are not necessarily accurate: sensors may break, systems can shut down, and information can be wrongly labeled. Open data has the potential to spread false information far from those who have the background knowledge to interpret or correct it. || When considering power dynamics between the public and the data controllers, it is important to note that open data are just one possible stage or avenue for public empowerment.
policy_relevance: Recommends careful selection of datasets, registration for data access, and responsive transparency to balance openness with accountability.

title: Toward an Architecture and Data Model to Enable Interoperability between Federated Mission Networks and IoT-Enabled Smart City Environments
thesis: Proposes an architecture and data model for interoperability between military federated mission networks and smart city IoT systems to enable military use of urban infrastructure for HADR.
key_quotes: The emergence of smart city initiatives in many areas of the world has led to rapid development and proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) technologies. Successful deployments of IoT have resulted in the military looking at the impacts and benefits of IoT, both for directly leveraging IoT within the military environment as well as to interface with smart city environments for urban operations such as humanitarian assistance and disaster response. || We propose an architecture and data model to enable interoperability between FMN and IoT networks in smart city environments. We review the various bottlenecks involved for such an environment and how a reference implementation can be set up to allow multiple partners to exchange data for sharing resources and provide better situational awareness. || The concepts discussed reuse and improvise upon the existing NATO and commercial IoT standards for faster adoption.
policy_relevance: Technical recommendations for enabling military-civilian data sharing in smart cities; suggests using MQTT and JSON for interoperability between military and civilian IoT systems in HADR contexts.

title: Leveraging Civilian IoT Infrastructures to Support Warfighting Activities in Urban Environments
thesis: Civilian Smart City IoT and Open Data can be integrated with military systems via Fog Computing to support HADR operations.
key_quotes: The increasing importance of urban environments in warfare, especially for counter-terrorism purposes, raises the opportunity to develop innovative military information systems that can easily integrate with civilian Smart City infrastructures and Open Data services to improve situational awareness. || Leveraging Civilian IoT Infrastructures to Support Warfighting Activities in Urban Environments || The emergence of Open Data services, that expose both raw data collected from IoT installations in Smart Cities as well as processed information, raises the opportunity to consider integrating military systems with civilian ones in support of military operations in urban environments.
policy_relevance: None

title: Performance measurement in smart city governance: A case study of an Egyptian city council
thesis: Performance measurement systems in smart city governance are institutionalized through cascading macro-micro pressures, with political and military influence shaping political decisions.
key_quotes: Institutionalised measurement systems or performance metrics play a powerful accounting role(s) in shaping and reshaping political decisions and military actions in the city council. || The political pressure from the military regime at the macro (state government) level institutionalises micro-organisational performance metrics utilised in smart city governance. || Performance measurements are seen in practice as a powerful accounting and accountability tool in managing public-private collaboration and hence the overall smart city governance.
policy_relevance: Recommends that city policymakers and regulators consider political and military pressures when implementing smart city governance and performance measurement systems; suggests other city councils may benefit from the New Cairo experience.

title: Secure the city, revitalize the zone: Smart urbanization in Camden, New Jersey
thesis: Camden's smart city surveillance and community policing strategy secured the city for zone-based neoliberal revitalization, but did not reduce crime as promised, instead producing new urban fragmentation.
key_quotes: Many of these policing technologies and tactics mirrored those used in the United States military’s counterinsurgency efforts in Iraq and Afghanistan (Petraeus, 2006), part of the ongoing militarization of cities worldwide (Graham, 2010). || The security apparatus had to be in place before businesses would come: urban regeneration was predicated on the installation of militarized, citywide surveillance. || The primary impact of the security apparatus was to advance economic ambitions in zones like the Camden Waterfront project. Massive tax breaks may provide the incentive for corporations to locate in the city, but presence of the security apparatus and its properties of social control justifies and secures the investment.
policy_relevance: Critiques the use of surveillance-first community policing as a prerequisite for urban revitalization, noting that it did not reduce crime but shifted perceptions. Recommends investment in residential neighborhoods and addressing root causes of poverty rather than relying on technological fixes.

title: A Focus on Electromobility within Smart City Solutions—Charging Stations, Renewable Energy, and Air Quality Monitoring
geography: Brno, Czech Republic and Glasgow, UK
thesis: This paper reviews electromobility, renewable energy, and air quality monitoring in smart cities, discussing their dual-use potential for civilian and military applications.
key_quotes: Smart cities are open domains for not only civil applications, but also for military purposes. || The infrastructure of smart cities can be considered as dual-use technology (civil and military) and should be able to help in times of disaster, security incidents, warfare activity... || The sensors in the city itself can bring more information about enemy activities or civil population movements.
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that dual-use potential should be considered during the conception and design of smart cities to enhance resilience in crises, but does not provide specific policy recommendations.

title: Public Trust and Political Legitimacy in the Smart City: A Reckoning for Technocracy
thesis: Examines how public trust and political legitimacy affect support for smart city endeavors in Hong Kong, revealing tensions between technocracy and democracy.
key_quotes: Technocracy ostensibly transcends the parlor games of politicians and power brokers to inform operable understandings about policy problems. || The technocratic imaginary stakes its political credibility on enhancing transparency, accountability, and effectiveness; these have been seen by governments as building blocks for strengthening trust and legitimacy. || This study's identification of statistically significant relationships between perceptions of legitimacy and smart cities support reflects a theme that is common across discussions about socio-technical imaginaries: loss of democratic control over policy processes captured by elite interests.
policy_relevance: None specific. Suggests further research on trust, legitimacy, and democratic participation in smart city governance.

title: Smart Cities, Surveillance and Speed in Imphal, Manipur
thesis: Enhanced surveillance under India's Smart Cities Mission in Imphal resonates with civilian authorities, armed forces, and citizens as a promise of development, despite decades of existing surveillance and counter-insurgency.
key_quotes: Surveillant assemblages resonate powerfully in Northeast Indian cities, where both vertical (e.g. military/paramilitary-civilian) and horizontal (e.g. neighbour-neighbour) surveillance has been woven into the fabric of urban life over decades. || Enhanced surveillance under the SCM is grafted into this existing surveillance assemblage. The population can be monitored as they move through urban space, and there are fewer glitches and blackspots, fewer human errors or head turns. || The extension of the SCM to the Northeast is part of a longer project of enrolling the frontier into national development by making legible, governable space.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the SCM's one-size-fits-all approach in frontier regions, suggesting that surveillance technologies map existing spatial politics rather than transform them. It implies the need for context-sensitive urban policy that accounts for militarized histories and ethnic tensions.

title: Smart Cities as "Big Brother Only to the Dialogue Masses": The Limits of Personal Privacy and Personal Surveillance
geography: Europe and North America (focus on Netherlands)
thesis: Smart city projects that process only non-personal data still pose surveillance risks, requiring a broader understanding of surveillance beyond individual identification.
key_quotes: The idea behind this novel approach to smartness can be condensed into a statement offered by one of Stratumseind Living Lab's actors: 'We are Big Brother only to the masses.' || In order to reveal the underlying dynamics of power and how these might lead to surveillance abuse—even, or especially, when surveillance is based on the processing of seemingly non-personal data—concrete surveillance practices and their logics need to be examined. || The securitizing logic of surveillance within the Stratumseind Living Lab and other smart cities is transforming public spaces into consumption spaces.
policy_relevance: The paper argues that data protection law's focus on personal data is inadequate for regulating smart city surveillance of aggregates, and calls for regulatory adaptation to address group privacy and the transformation of public space.

title: Radio Frequency IoT Sensors in Military Operations in a Smart City
thesis: This paper presents the development of a low-cost RF IoT sensor using COTS software defined radios for military spectrum monitoring and tracking in smart cities.
key_quotes: This paper presents work performed by the NATO IST-147 'Military Applications of Internet of Things' group to explore the potential to exploit civilian Internet of Things (IoT) software defined radio infrastructure as radio frequency sensors for military operations. || Several scenarios are considered ranging from spectrum analysis, direction finding, and information fusion/tracking. || With the ability to leverage multiple software defined sensor sources from the Internet of Things, using directional modulation in the physical layer becomes a valuable asset as, by just replacing the antenna stage of already deployed radios, it substantively enhances security of the transmitted data while also preventing detection and spoofing of your desired sensors or other contributing network nodes.
policy_relevance: None

title: Decision-support system for safety and security assessment and management in smart cities
thesis: A Decision Support System for anti-terrorist urban security in smart cities, integrating threat analysis, evacuation, and traffic monitoring to support real-time decision-making.
key_quotes: This paper introduces a comprehensive Decision Support System developed as part of the S4AllCitites project, designed to seamlessly integrate with existing legacy systems in Smart Cities. || The system empowers public and private security operators with real time decision support capabilities during both prevention and intervention stages of potential attacks. || By integrating with existing smart city systems, the proposed DSS empowers decision-makers and operators during the planning and response phases, providing proactive threat anticipation and facilitating effective decision-making processes.
policy_relevance: The system can inform urban planning and security design, integrating with CPTED (Crime Prevention through Environmental Design) principles to proactively incorporate security measures into smart city infrastructure.

title: Contesting Digital Futures: Urban Politics, Alternative Economies, and the Movement for Technological Sovereignty in Barcelona
thesis: Explores alternative digital development practices of the technological sovereignty movement in Barcelona, advancing prefigurative urban politics and postcapitalist economies beyond critiques of the smart city.
key_quotes: the algorithms that process such data are hidden from view, subject to intellectual property protections. || smart city programs turn political issues of urban governance into problems with 'technical' solutions. || the TS movement offers an example of how urban residents can exercise political agency through forms of creative experimentation with digital technologies—performing alternative economic practices and enacting forms of radical democracy against the 'post-political' turn in urban governance.
policy_relevance: Discusses municipal government support for technological sovereignty, including migration to open-source systems, ethical digital standards, and subsidies for cooperative enterprises. Notes limitations of state power and electoral cycles.

title: Improving network resources allocation in smart cities video surveillance
thesis: Proposes a multilevel resources broker for heterogeneous networks to allocate resources for video surveillance in smart cities and military borderline security, balancing QoS and cost.
key_quotes: In this article, a heterogeneous network scenario is considered to implement a multi-purpose real time video surveillance application which can be applied to both smart cities and military surveillance such as borderline security. || Since the analyzed scenario can be applied to military surveillance, a variety of kinds of resources are present. Since the main scenario to be analyzed is a military borderline security application, a variety of MNOs and technologies are considered to be available. || The availability of a LSA pool of military frequencies is also considered as network resources to be allocated whenever necessary.
policy_relevance: None

title: Illiberal smart urbanism? Lessons from the politics of state-led smart securitisation in Miskolc, Hungary
thesis: Smart urbanism in Miskolc is overtly politicized under an illiberal regime, using CCTV surveillance to consolidate right-wing populist securitization, challenging post-political accounts.
key_quotes: In contrast to mainstream post-political understandings of smart urbanism, Miskolc’s smart surveillance project is wrapped up in an explicitly right-wing populist, and in certain respects racialised social ordering campaign. || The smart cameras are a key manifestation of this populist politics but they also reproduce the illiberal smart city through engineering a new form of normative consensus around securitisation. || Our effort to confront the unprecedented begins with the recognition that we hunt the puppet master, not the puppet.
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that state-led smart urbanism in illiberal contexts can entrench exclusionary policies, and that local governments may be forced to maintain securitization due to electoral pressures, limiting emancipatory alternatives.

title: Speculative futures: Cities, data, and governance beyond smart urbanism
thesis: Urban big data governance enacts speculative futures that anticipate and securitize against risks, but cannot divest itself of existing socio-spatial inequalities, projecting them forward.
key_quotes: EMOTIVE is furthermore interesting insofar as it is demonstrative of the ways in which corporate and state forms of governance (and governmentality) are increasingly difficult to separate as data and security have become progressively imbricated in an ever-intensifying '(big) data-security assemblage' which privileges and enables data-driven forms of securitization (Aradau and Blanke, 2015). || The urban derivative abstracts extant inequalities into algorithmic projections of possible urban futures, such that enactments of algorithmic governmentality reassemble the city in its own geographically uneven image. || Insofar as (urban) big data look to the future, it cannot but anticipate socio-spatially stratified cities. This is because the security calculus is dependent on the urban derivative which, contra Amoore's (2011, 2014) theorization of the data derivative, is not indifferent to actual conditions on the ground.
policy_relevance: Critiques predictive policing and sentiment analytics as reinforcing urban inequalities; suggests that data-driven governance should be attentive to representation biases and the persistence of socio-spatial stratification. Notes the potential for counter-data projects like the Citizens Police Data Project to invert power imbalances.

title: 중국 인공지능산업의 발전과 사회적 규제 논의 - 개인정보 보호와 디지털권위주의를 중심으로 -
thesis: Analysis of China's AI regulation shows that privacy protection is strengthened for corporate misuse but government surveillance for national security remains unregulated.
key_quotes: 디지털 권위주의는 AI를 포함한 디지털 기술을 활용하여 국가 이데올로기를 강화하거나 시민에 대한 통제와 감시를 일상화하여 정치적 통제를 확대하는 체제를 말한다. || 스마트시티는 정보통신기술(ICT)과 데이터 컴퓨팅, 영상인식 등 AI기술을 기반으로 도시기반시설을 촘촘히 연결하여 치안, 교통, 행정, 교육 등에 첨단 인프라가 적용된 지능형 도시를 말한다. || AI 기술이 전쟁, 테러, 범죄 등에 악용될 경우 그 피해는 심각할 것이다.
policy_relevance: Suggests China needs to develop social regulation to minimize AI's negative effects, especially government surveillance, to gain international trust.

title: Computational Intelligence Methods for Green Technology and Sustainable Development: Proceedings of the International Conference GTSD2024, Volume 1
thesis: This edited volume presents proceedings from GTSD2024, covering computational intelligence for green technology and sustainable development across diverse engineering applications.
policy_relevance: None

title: Fabrication of space: The design of everyday life in South Korean Songdo
thesis: Songdo's smart city design is a hybrid fabrication of space enabled by the fusion of 'seeing like a state' and 'seeing like a corporation', normalizing surveillance and social control through semi-gated communities.
key_quotes: Securitised by the ubiquitous digital tools of centralised surveillance, First World dispenses with hard borders and rests instead on a concept of ‘soft’ gatedness || The provision of safety is shifted entirely to the apatu's privately run central security office and the main lobbies of buildings that one cannot enter unannounced. ... We have 400 CCTVs in our block || Seeing like a state and seeing like a corporation overlap in their common vision of making society legible and thus manageable, whereby systems of control and extraction of profit can be more efficiently consolidated and normalised
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that the hybrid state-corporate model of urban governance normalizes surveillance and reduces public space, with implications for urban planning and the need for more participatory and less securitized approaches.

title: The Challenge of Big Data and Data Science
thesis: Reviews societal impacts of big data and data science for political science, including smart cities, cyber-warfare, and ethical challenges.
key_quotes: Big data and data science are transforming the world in ways that spawn new concerns for social scientists, such as the impacts of the internet on citizens and the media, the repercussions of smart cities, the possibilities of cyber-warfare and cyber-terrorism... || Because the decisions about what data are collected, how they are processed, and how they are used all involve choices, often influenced by who has power and who does not, these systems are inherently political. They can easily become technocratic, overly influenced by corporate interests, and perhaps most alarmingly, the basis for the 'panoptic' city... || A number of writers (Harcourt 2007, Mbadiwe 2018, Williams et al. 2018) have worried that algorithms used to assign bail, decide on sentences, or place prisoners in various levels of detention rely on predictions that are not causal, that reproduce stereotypes, and that exacerbate racial biases.
policy_relevance: Discusses ethical issues of algorithmic decision-making (bail, sentencing, police stops, campaign mobilization) and calls for political scientists to be involved in designing social institutions and policies. No specific policy recommendations.

title: The Future Possibilities and Security Challenges of City Digitalization
thesis: City digitalization is highly individual and while current platforms visualize data, they lack advanced AI functions; security risks and military dual-use potential must be considered from the start.
key_quotes: The technical design of a smart city should also be considered from the perspective of ensuring the defence of the state from two different perspectives: Misuse of the technical infrastructure by the enemy to support their attack... The use of the smart city’s technical infrastructure to support the defence of its own territory when attacked by the enemy. || The use of the smart city infrastructure by the military is, according to [69], possible in different areas: Sensors deployed in buildings can provide data on air quality, chemical/smoke, radiation, and gas to indicate various types of chemical leaks, explosions, and hostile activities in areas. || The architecture of the smart city and army technologies would need to be developed in mutual compliance to avoid interoperability issues. Only then will it be possible to take advantage of all the benefits that cooperation between smart city technologies and the army offers.
policy_relevance: Recommends that security and possible misuse be considered from the beginning of hardware and software design; essential or critical infrastructure systems must comply with relevant legislation; smart city and military technologies should be developed in mutual compliance for interoperability.

title: Integrated mass surveillance system for large scale events
thesis: Presents a crowdsensing-based mass surveillance system for large events to monitor crowd dynamics and enable targeted interventions by authorities.
key_quotes: We have developed an integrated mass surveillance system based on crowdsensing data, where the system helps authorities and organizers in information gathering about the actual dynamics of the crowd. || If the organizers and authorities can obtain valid information about the crowd dynamics, they would be able to perform quick and targeted interventions. || The system in default does not send alert messages directly to the participants as it could lead to even greater panic.
policy_relevance: None

title: How Fear of Crime Affects Needs for Privacy & Safety: Acceptance of Surveillance Technologies in Smart Cities
thesis: Individual perceived crime threat significantly influences acceptance of surveillance technologies in urban environments, with higher fear correlating with lower privacy concerns in public spaces.
key_quotes: people usually do not know, which of their actions are monitored or how or for what purpose surveillance data is further processed and used || the assessment of individual privacy and safety needs provides an explanation for the identified acceptance patterns. In public spaces, people have a higher need for safety, i.e. they 'sacrifice' their privacy rights for a higher safety from potential crime assaults || the predominantly technology-centered planning of infrastructural city concepts, without integrating citizens into the decision-making processes, seems not sufficient to cover persons’ attitudes regarding safety and privacy concerns in the context of smart cities
policy_relevance: Suggests that urban surveillance planning should consider citizen diversity in perceived crime threat, and that ethical-normative approaches should be complemented by user-focused perspectives.

title: Introduction
thesis: Megacities require new intelligence frameworks integrating civilian and military data for situational awareness and stability prediction.
key_quotes: Therefore, there is a need for a common intelligence framework that captures military operations, urban operations, emergency response operations, and city behavior. By creating such a framework, the sharing of information and common understanding of potential instabilities can be recognized and communicated across interested parties. || Both the US Army and the World Bank are studying megacities, in an effort to define indicators through which to manage or describe these urban environments. || Based on the rise of the Internet of Things and Smart City technologies, future intelligence techniques for megacities will be data focused.
policy_relevance: Suggests need for a common intelligence framework integrating military and civilian data for megacity stability, implying cross-sector coordination challenges.

title: Realtime Urbanism: The Architecture of Packets, Pixels, and Neurons
thesis: Realtime urbanism is a mode of spatial governance emerging from computation, communication, and immersive media, operating across urban space with minimal delay, rooted in imperial infrastructures with contemporary consequences of violence and control.
key_quotes: Realtime systems produce a latency-driven epistemology, naturalize control as responsiveness, and collapse deliberation into automation. || Realtime urbanism is not neutral. It is a political formation rooted in imperial infrastructures with contemporary consequences. || The ability to sense, model, and intervene with minimal delay defines the current trajectory of military, entertainment, and urban systems. Realtime is the shared operational condition that enables all three.
policy_relevance: Calls for architecture to confront complicity, reject techno-solutionism, and align with movements of refusal and emancipation; no specific policy recommendations.

title: Studying Surveillance AI-cologies in Public Safety: How AI Is in the World and the World in AI
thesis: The paper argues that AI-aided surveillance in public safety forms complex 'surveillance AI-cologies' requiring a quintuple helix and ELSA framework for democratic governance, exemplified by a Living Lab in Scheveningen.
key_quotes: Using AI in public safety might carry the increased risk of contributing to opaque decision making, structural inequalities, and the further manifestation of systemic injustices. || It is crucial to problematise the technological impetus not only to avoid unnecessary investments in the rush to implement AI but also to avoid other (unintended) societal effects. || The development of democratically controlled AI surveillance requires the systematic consideration of ethical, legal, and social aspects (ELSA) within the quintuple helix (public, private, civil society, academia, nature).
policy_relevance: The paper advocates for democratic control of AI surveillance, matching investment in technological infrastructure with democratic infrastructure, and considering 'No Surveillance AI-cologies' as a valid option. It calls for inclusive stakeholder engagement and ethical oversight.

title: Hidden in Plain Sight: Toward a Smart Future in Eindhoven
thesis: Examines the pervasive, often hidden deployment of smart technologies in Eindhoven, revealing how citizens are subjected to data collection and surveillance without consent, and questions the normalization of mass-surveillance.
key_quotes: Traces of such a proliferation of 'smartness' appear dotted throughout the city in the form of cameras and sensors, without much disclosure regarding who owns them and what they are used for. || Eindhoven’s citizens are subjected to various data-collection systems and living-lab experiments without their knowledge or agreement, as well as without any idea of the potential consequences and implications. || the only way to opt-out of participation is to opt-out of the city.
policy_relevance: Highlights the need for transparency and regulation in smart city data collection; criticizes the voluntary sensor registry as ineffective and calls for addressing the normalization of surveillance.

title: THE ROLE OF ADDITIONAL INFORMATION IN OBTAINING INFORMATION
thesis: Additional information transmitted in public communication can be obtained via OSINT, illustrated through an online game.
key_quotes: In public communication the destination of the information is not a specific person or object. Therefore, additional information can be obtained by anyone. || The technology of Open Source Intelligence is one of the basic elements of the social engineering information palette. || The game's summary is an example of how examining transmitted information from other angles can influence information acquisition.
policy_relevance: None

title: Surveillance, race, and social sorting in the United Arab Emirates
thesis: Surveillance technologies in the UAE are not race-neutral but reinforce ethno-racial hierarchies and state control, embedded in colonial legacies and global War on Terror networks.
key_quotes: Surveillance technologies are today easily commodified and circulate through the private surveillance industry. In the wake of the WoT, the rampant privatisation of warfare, from the use of Private Military and Security Companies (PMSCs), logistics firms for the housing and feeding of troops, to contracting private surveillance firms, has helped to both grow and imbed this private surveillance industry well beyond conflict zones. || Despite claims to being race-neutral and scientific, surveillance technologies have an embedded racial bias and operate according to context to (re)produce forms of state control and racial social relations. || The biometric ID itself becomes the node, which determines all interactions with the state, integrating every relation, even with basic infrastructures like hospitals, telecommunications, and water, into its remit.
policy_relevance: Critiques the transfer of surveillance technologies and counterterror legislation from Western states to the UAE, highlighting how such transfers reinforce authoritarian governance and racial hierarchies. Recommends moving beyond a focus on liberal democracies to examine non-Western contexts.

title: Kommersiell sporing – nasjonal risiko
thesis: Commercial digital tracking and sale of personal data pose national security risks as they can be exploited by foreign powers for espionage, sabotage, and subversion.
key_quotes: Datasettenes digitale natur medfører større detaljgrad, maskinlesbarhet optimalisert for automatisering, lange tidsserier, sanntidspotensial og mindre ressurskrevende datainnhenting sammenlignet med analoge metoder. || Kommersiell digital overvåkning har blitt så omfattende at det medfører en stor datalekkasje inn i et uoversiktlig, globalt marked. || Artikkelen vil vise eksempler på hvordan data har blitt anvendt for etterretning og sporing av enkeltpersoner, tilrettelegging for dataangrep, kartlegging av skjermede lokalisasjoner, samt som et verktøy i påvirkningsoperasjoner rettet mot grupper.
policy_relevance: Argues that strong privacy legislation should be viewed as a collective security tool, not a bureaucratic straightjacket, and that data control and privacy are national security issues.

title: Cybersecurity as a Politikum: Implications of Security Discourses for Infrastructures
thesis: Security is an ambiguous, contested concept; its framing in discourse shapes ICT infrastructure governance and access, making cybersecurity a political matter (Politikum).
key_quotes: Security is a contested concept rather than a fixed goal. The way it is conveyed and understood (i.e. in terms of threat models and trusted parties) shapes how technologies and technological infrastructures are designed and operated. || When something is framed as a security issue, it can motivate actions which have structural impacts on an ICT infrastructure. Within governance processes, cybersecurity arguments can justify certain actions and practices which have effects on the overall infrastructure and can further or counter other, non-security related aspects. || The political role of framing becomes clearer when we look at the function of security arguments within (infrastructure) governance. On the one hand, framing a security issue in a certain way is a feasible tool to justify certain activities. On the other hand, framing something as a security issue can justify extraordinary measures that would otherwise be deemed undesirable.
policy_relevance: The paper argues for increased transparency and democratic control in security decision-making, and suggests that making security frames explicit can improve communication and accountability in infrastructure governance.

title: Urban military geographies: New directions in the (re)production of space, militarism, and the urban
geography: global (primarily European and North American cities)
thesis: This review uses Lefebvre's spatial triad to conceptualize urban military geographies in peacetime, showing how cities are privileged sites for reproducing militarism and how military presence shapes urban space.
key_quotes: control technologies developed for military purposes have become more intertwined with the new architectures of urban life and the 'spaces of discipline' (Foucault, 1991), creating a strong link between citizenship, consumption and militarism. || the discursive and material construction of smart cities (Vanolo, 2014; Wiig, 2018; Wiig & Wyly, 2016) have supported the development of hybrid systems that enable the tracking of citizens' habits and behaviours. || these processes, which combine military and civilian activities, respond to a twofold need within contemporary cities: firstly, to mobilise control infrastructures for purposes of defence and preparation for war; secondly, to support processes of valorisation and financialisation of urban time and space, through surveillance tools originally developed by the armed forces.
policy_relevance: None

title: Your face is not new to me – Regulating the surveillance power of facial recognition technologies
geography: Europe (with references to US and Asia)
thesis: Facial recognition technologies used by law enforcement can be regulated proportionately under EU data protection law and the AI Act, rather than banned outright, to balance surveillance benefits with fundamental rights.
key_quotes: FRTs are one of the cutting-edge applications of artificial intelligence and big data for surveillance purposes. The uses of these biometric technologies are widespread in our cities. However, they may result in serious abuses against the rights of people and minorities, or even in new kinds of mass surveillance. || FRTs produce an 'informatization of the body' (Van Der Ploeg, 2005), whereby body parts are objectivised and become direct sources of digital information for automated external controls to which the person is subjected. || The EDPB and the EDPS have also stressed that it is crucial to ensure clarity concerning the relationship between the Proposal and existing legislation (EDPB & EDPS, 2021, §15).
policy_relevance: Recommends regulating FRTs under EU data protection law and the AI Act, with proportionality as the guiding principle; calls for clear rules on legal basis, data retention, bias mitigation, and independent authorisation for use by law enforcement.

title: A Crowdsensing Platform for Mass Surveillance
thesis: Presents a crowdsensing-based mass surveillance system using mobile phone data to monitor crowd dynamics in real time for event safety.
key_quotes: We have developed an integrated mass surveillance system based on crowdsensing data, where the system helps authorities and organizers in information gathering about the actual dynamics of the crowd. || The authorities need reliable surveillance systems which can provide better monitoring solutions to understand the movement of the crowd in a real time manner. || The vast majority of visitors of today's large events already have a mobile device... Data from these sensors are collectable and by processing them valuable information can be obtained.
policy_relevance: None

title: URBAN OPERATING SYSTEMS: Diagramming the City
thesis: Urban Operating Systems transfer rationalities from military and corporate domains to the city, constructing a new urban diagram of control based on functional simplification and heterogeneous reintegration.
key_quotes: This article aims to examine the emerging Urban OS, tracing its historical roots within military and corporate domains whilst also establishing how its contemporary application may generate new relations and embody a new logic of urban control. || Drawing on rationalities and techniques originally developed in the interface between the defence, corporate and IT sectors, Urban OS prioritize a highly technocratic style of integrative urban control. || The Urban OS, as an essential component of the smart city, emerges as a new urban diagram which 'does not function to represent, even something real, but rather constructs a real that is to come, a new type of reality' (Deleuze and Guattari, 1987: 142).
policy_relevance: The paper calls for scrutiny of the epistemological underpinnings of computational urbanism and suggests that the progressive potential of smart cities depends on subjecting their modes of calculation to democratic debate. It does not offer specific policy recommendations.

title: Future Cities: Trends and Implications
thesis: Examines future urban trends (smart cities, environment, infrastructure, demographics, actors) and their military implications for UK operations, highlighting opportunities and risks.
