key_quotes: The unmaking of urban life is shown to be not collateral, but integral to a strategic logic aimed at disabling civic infrastructure, displacing populations, and erasing the viability of future sovereignty. || Urbicide, in this sense, names a modality of structural elimination deeply embedded in broader regimes of domination, whether nationalist, colonial, or imperial. || The destruction of public archives, municipal records, and cultural landmarks suggests a deeper goal: the erasure of memory and continuity. Gaza is not merely being bombed—it is being unmade as a space of collective identity and political potential.
policy_relevance: Calls for further research on post-urbicidal urban recovery, politics of memory, and spatial justice in colonial and postcolonial contexts. No specific policy recommendations.

title: Urbicide in Israel’s War on Gaza: Architecture of Erasure and the Unmaking of Urban Life (2023–2025)
thesis: Urbicide in Gaza (2023–2025) is a deliberate settler-colonial strategy of spatial erasure, not collateral damage, aimed at dismantling urban life, memory, and sovereignty.
key_quotes: Hospitals, schools, mosques, media institutions, and universities have been struck under the rationale of dual-use or symbolic alignment with resistance. || The destruction of Gaza’s built environment between 2023 and 2025 constitutes what may be termed a Spatial Nakba—an intentional strategy of architectural erasure and forced spatial reconfiguration. || Urbicide in Gaza between 2023 and 2025 operates not as a byproduct of war but as a central pillar of Israel’s military and spatial strategy.
policy_relevance: Calls for further research on post-urbicidal urban recovery, politics of memory, and spatial justice; notes that reconstruction is denied through permit systems and material restrictions.

title: Constructing Urbicide in the Modern War on Terror: Surveillance and the Politics of Categorical Exclusion in Public Space in Xinjiang
Radar the Next Generation Sensors as Robots
thesis: Proposes a futuristic 'Sensors as Robots' concept for autonomous, collaborative ISR sensor systems for military and civilian applications.
key_quotes: Future military and civilian requirements will be stressing and will require innovative sensors and sensor configurations. || Sensors as Robots technology will help to accelerate this process for both military and civilian applications. || we foresee military applications in the vein of the surveillance of hostile urban battlefield situations as well as monitoring functions inherent to peacekeeping activities; civilian applications such as crop production assessment/management and WIC assessment/management; industrial applications that include factory smoke emissions monitoring, production assembly assessment and management, facility management, and inventory shipment and tracking.
policy_relevance: None

title: Leviathan's Architect: Urbicide, Urban Renewal, and the Right to the City in Turkish Kurdistan
geography: Turkey (Southeastern Turkey, Turkish Kurdistan: Sur/Diyarbakır, Nusaybin)
thesis: Post-conflict razing and reconstruction in Turkish Kurdistan is a form of securitized development that remakes urban space to erase Kurdish identity and impose state control, but residents resist through memory projects and cultural activism.
key_quotes: Urbicide can mean 'place annihilation,' or the 'destruction of major features of the urban environment and civil ecology.' It can also mean wrecking the idea of the city as a diverse, tolerant, livable space. || The state has harnessed tabula rasa reconstruction for its own ends, displacing and dispossessing residents as it seeks to remake the physical as well as social fabric of Kurdish-majority cities. || The new designs instead cultivate life patterns that are more individualistic and less gregarious. ... Vernacular and communal architecture have been replaced with housing units and apartment towers that cut people off from their neighbors and integrate them into state agencies and mortgage regimes.
policy_relevance: The paper calls for a new political language for planning and design that hinges on history and inclusion rather than Realpolitik, and highlights the need for effective investigations and accountability for civilian deaths during curfews.

title: Time-series satellite remote sensing reveals gradually increasing war damage in the Gaza Strip
thesis: Integrating deep learning with high-resolution satellite data enables near real-time detection of war damage, revealing progressively increasing destruction in Gaza from Oct 2023 to Mar 2024.
key_quotes: We developed an automated method to detect war damage to buildings and farmland and locate missile craters using these data. || We found 3747 missile craters across five governorates in the Gaza Strip, which serve as a historical record in determining accurate estimates of potential unexploded ordnance (UXO) locations and assisting in demining and chemical decontamination. || These first-time findings highlight the urgent need for an immediate ceasefire to prevent further damage and support the release of hostages and subsequent reconstruction efforts.
policy_relevance: Calls for immediate ceasefire and reconstruction; methodology offers cost-effective, scalable approach for conflict monitoring and post-war reconstruction planning.

title: Factored reasoning for monitoring dynamic team and goal formation
thesis: Presents a particle filtering algorithm that reasons locally about unit positions and globally about team structure and goals to detect threats in asymmetric urban warfare.
key_quotes: The setting for our study is an asymmetric urban warfare environment in which uncoordinated or loosely coordinated units may attempt to attack an important target. The task is to detect a threat such as an ambush, as early as possible. || We attempt to provide decision-makers with early warnings, by simultaneously monitoring the positions of units, the teams to which they belong, and the goals of units. || In our experiments, we use a map of central Baghdad that has 119 streets and 79 intersections.
policy_relevance: None

title: The Wayfarer modular navigation payload for intelligent robot infrastructure
geography: United States (Burlington, MA, and urban/natural test environments)
thesis: This paper presents the development of a modular navigation payload for the iRobot PackBot to enable fully autonomous urban reconnaissance missions for military applications.
key_quotes: iRobot Corporation is a world leader in developing mobile robots for combat operations. Our man-portable PackBot Scout robots have been used to explore Taliban caves in Afghanistan and insurgent strongholds in Najaf. || The Wayfarer Project is an applied research effort that is tightly focused on developing robust techniques for autonomous reconnaissance in urban environments. || We are developing a modular navigation payload that will provide urban navigation capabilities for the PackBot or any other robot using the PackBot payload interface.
policy_relevance: None

title: An Advanced Telereflexive Tactical Response Robot
thesis: Describes a tactical response robot for law enforcement and urban warfare with reflexive teleoperation and human-centered mapping.
key_quotes: ROBART III is intended as an advanced demonstration platform for non-lethal tactical response, extending the concepts of reflexive teleoperation into the realm of coordinated weapons control (i.e., sensor-aided control of mobility, camera, and weapon functions) in law enforcement and urban warfare scenarios. || The system is able to confront intruders with a laser-sighted tranquilizer dart gun, and automatically track a moving target with the use of various sensors. || A human-centered mapping scheme ensures more accurate first-time interpretation of navigational landmarks as the robot builds its world model, while orthogonal navigation exploits the fact that the majority of man-made structures are characterized by parallel and orthogonal walls.
policy_relevance: None

title: Rapid assessment of large-scale urban destruction in conflict zones using hypergraph-based visual-structural machine learning
thesis: Proposes ViT2G, a visual-graph machine learning framework using hypergraphs and Vision Transformers to rapidly assess urban damage from war using satellite imagery, outperforming traditional methods.
key_quotes: In an era marked by increasing geopolitical conflicts, the accurate and swift assessment of urban damage in war-affected areas is crucial for implementing effective emergency responses and sustainable recovery planning. || advanced forms of warfare, such as missile attacks and drone strikes, have targeted civilian infrastructure such as residential buildings, schools and hospitals, exacerbating the humanitarian situation. || The ViT2G framework employs a novel approach by utilizing hypergraph structures and Vision Transformers (ViT), enabling a more detailed representation of urban areas than traditional graph-based methods.
policy_relevance: Potential policy relevance for humanitarian organisations and urban planners for emergency response and reconstruction planning in conflict zones, but no specific policy recommendations are discussed.

title: An automated security response robot
Algorithmic War: Everyday Geographies of the War on Terror
thesis: Algorithmic security technologies in the war on terror blur military, commercial, and civil spheres, producing violent geographies through pre-emptive calculation and targeting in everyday life.
key_quotes: It is not that algorithmic techniques have their origins strictly in the military domain (though, as we will see, many of them do), nor that society is strictly undergoing renewed militarization, but that security practices oscillate back and forth across different domains. || The promise that algorithmic calculations held out to the commercial authorities of the 1990s—to enable surveillance from a distance, to make market judgements in advance, to generate patterns of normal and atypical consumer behaviour—is now being re-made in the context of state security desires. || The association rules of the algorithm claim precisely to identify associations, to connect together here and there, to link that location of suspicion and this embodied risk, to suture together the forces of war in one place and the possibility of threat in the spaces of everyday life.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the privatization of security and the transfer of commercial data-mining techniques to state security, suggesting that these practices conceal violence and discrimination. It implies a need for greater transparency and democratic oversight of algorithmic security systems, but does not offer specific policy recommendations.

title: Unplug and Play: Manufacturing Collapse in Gaza
thesis: Infrastructural networks in post-disengagement Gaza function as geopolitical sites of spatial control and biopolitical tools to regulate and suppress life, manufacturing a regulated humanitarian collapse.
key_quotes: Infrastructure networks are thus the life support systems of modern societies, source of their vitality and yet source of its own fragility and manipulation. || The destruction of the power plant added to, and enhanced, what already was a chronic dependency on a legacy of colonial infrastructure used to manipulate and regulate the life of the colonized. || The concept of infrastructural violence provides a particularly useful lens through which to study the systematic politics of spatial reengineering that undoes the ordinary geographies of everyday life by generating and unfolding a hostile topography of infrastructure networks for purposes of population management and repression as well as territorial segregation and control.
policy_relevance: The paper argues that targeting civilian infrastructure constitutes war crimes and collective punishment under international law, and calls for expanding the referents of political violence to include the material fabric of urban life. It highlights the role of human rights organizations in challenging these practices.

title: Constructing resilience through security and surveillance: The politics, practices and tensions of security-driven resilience
thesis: Security-driven resilience, drawing on surveillance and military technologies, generates tensions between state security and community cohesion that may subvert resilience's founding principles.
key_quotes: military technologies have been increasingly utilized in civic spaces, posing a series of questions about social control, citizenship and the ability to construct community resilience in local areas amidst state attempts to label the same areas as 'dangerous'. || Of the high-specification surveillance cameras in 'Project Champion', 150 came equipped with Automated Number Plate Recognition (ANPR) capability, developed from former military technology that could automatically monitor all vehicles entering and exiting the areas; whilst a further 72 covert cameras were camouflaged within street signs, furniture and other features of the urban landscape. || the opacity of many security-driven resilience initiatives, the politicized nature of hierarchical relationships within resilience practice, and the specific politics that such arrangements produce mean such aspirations are not always easy to realize.
policy_relevance: Highlights need for transparent governance and community engagement in security-driven resilience; warns against co-opting local safety agendas for national security; describes erosion of police-community trust as a key consequence.

title: Postmortem city: Towards an urban geopolitics
thesis: The paper argues that warfare and political violence are intimately woven into the fabric of cities and urban planning, and calls for an urban geopolitics to confront the militarisation of urban space.
key_quotes: War and the city have intimately shaped each other throughout urban and military history. "There is ... a direct reciprocity between war and cities", writes the geographer Ken Hewitt. "The latter are the more thoroughgoing constructs of collective life, containing the definitive human places. War is the most thorough-going or consciously prosecuted occasion of collective violence that destroys places." (Hewitt, 1983, p. 258). || Even a leading US Air Force planner had to concede that this direct targeting of so-called 'dual-use' (military/civilian) electrical infrastructure in 1991 "shut down water purification and sewage treatment plants. As a result, epidemics of gastroenteritis, cholera, and typhoid broke out, leading to as many as 100,000 civilian deaths and the doubling of infant mortality rates" (Rizer, 2001). || Urban terrorism and state counter-terror tend to be umbilically connected. In the end, they tend, tragically, to be self-perpetuating in an endless circle of intensifying atrocity.
policy_relevance: Calls for urban social science to confront militarisation of urban space and develop an urban geopolitics. Advocates for nurturing multicultural urban spaces as a normative response to fundamentalisms.

title: From urban catastrophe to 'model' city? Politics, security and development in post-conflict Kigali
thesis: Kigali's transformation from post-genocide catastrophe to a 'model' city was achieved through political consolidation, donor support, and securitisation strategies that tightly control urban space, but this may suppress underlying conflicts.
key_quotes: The government’s overriding concern with national security issues, combined with its need for legitimacy, has led to sustained efforts to create a city that is tightly controlled through a range of strategies that project it as a ‘model’ space, both domestically and internationally. || The emphasis on order and urban reorganisation to some degree parallels the rural social engineering discussed elsewhere. || The expropriations in the name of the Master Plan discussed earlier have proved highly controversial, and the relative absence of social violence in the city should not obscure the use of actual or threatened violence by the state in relation to these kinds of state-society interactions.
policy_relevance: The paper implies that post-conflict urban governance must balance security with inclusive civic engagement to avoid suppressing conflicts that may resurface. It highlights risks of elite-driven planning that excludes the poor.

title: When Life Itself is War: On the Urbanization of Military and Security Doctrine
thesis: New ideologies of permanent war are radically intensifying the militarization of urban life through the 'new military urbanism', which normalizes the targeting of everyday urban sites, circulations, and populations.
key_quotes: The new military urbanism's second foundation is the fusing and blurring of civilian and military applications of control, surveillance, communications, simulation and targeting technologies. This is not surprising given that control technologies with military origins are now fundamental bases for virtually all acts of digitally mediated urban life and consumption in advanced industrial cities, and that commercial modifications of such technologies are in turn being widely re-appropriated by the military. || French philosopher Gilles Deleuze (1992) famously termed contemporary societies 'societies of control'. Because networked electronic control and surveillance devices are now distributed through society, Deleuze argued that everyday urban life is now modulated by a sense of ever-present tracking, scrutiny and electronic calculation. || Defined as political violence intentionally designed to erase or 'kill' cities, urbicidal violence can involve the ethno-nationalist targeting of spaces of cosmopolitan mixing (as in the Balkans in the 1990s); the systematic devastation of the means of modern urban living (as with the de-electrification of Iraq in 1991, the 2006–08 siege of Gaza or the 2006 attack on Lebanon); or the simple erasure of those demonized people and places that are cast out as unmodern, barbarian, unclean, pathological or subhuman.
policy_relevance: Calls for critical urban research to expose and confront the normalization of the new military urbanism, and to explore how social and political mobilizations can obstruct and challenge these norms. Suggests need for comparative work on how securitization is refracted through different national and urban contexts.

title: Network-Centric Violence, Critical Infrastructure and the Urbanization of Security
thesis: Contemporary urban warfare targets critical infrastructure because it is constitutive of metropolitan life, revealing a reciprocal dynamic of urban securitization.
key_quotes: The sanctions regime did not target infrastructure per se, it prevented the reconstruction, repair or maintenance of a number of infrastructural sites on the basis that they comprised 'dual use' facilities of potential importance to the Iraqi military. || Targeting critical infrastructure in order to disrupt urbanity thus comprises a historically specific form of violence. || Network-centric warfare was conceived in the post-Cold War period as an element of the so-called Revolution in Military Affairs (RMA). It refers to a doctrine based on domination of the information spectrum supported by the use of precision munitions, mobile forces, and accurate real-time modelling of enemy forces and infrastructures.
policy_relevance: The paper argues that securitization of urban infrastructure (hardening, surveillance) is insufficient because it protects material substrate but not networked interconnectivity, and calls for a security studies that appreciates the complex ecology of metropolitan subjectivity.

title: EXPERIENCES OF URBAN MILITARISM: Spatial Stigma, Ruins and Everyday Life
thesis: Examines how poor Palestinians in Lydda experience spatial stigma and militarism through an uneasy combination of denigration, care, and historical awareness.
key_quotes: Urban geopolitics has compellingly connected cities and broader geopolitical processes, identified cities as key targets of military interventions, and conceptualized the destruction of buildings as a distinct form of political violence. || The ruins and empty spaces of the old Arab city are some of the visible material traces of the mass displacement of Palestinians in July 1948, when the Israeli army expelled all the 20,000 Palestinian residents of the city... || By studying the interplay between interpretive and affective responses to a built environment that has been targeted and 'blemished' by militarism, this article resonates with Mona Harb's recent call to 'diversify urban studies' perspectives on the city at war'.
policy_relevance: None. The paper calls for a new perspective on urban militarism focused on everyday life but does not offer specific policy recommendations.

title: Policing Development: Urban Renewal as Neo-liberal Security Strategy
thesis: Post-apartheid policing in Cape Town townships, driven by neoliberal security ideology, reproduces aggressive apartheid-era policing, securitizes urban renewal, and undermines development by containing rather than addressing root causes of crime.
key_quotes: current approaches to urban renewal risk exacerbating social instability by reproducing aggressive forms of policing associated with the apartheid era. || Policing on the Cape Flats today is perhaps best understood not an example of bad policing or misdirected policing but, rather, from the point of view of the neo-liberal city, necessary policing. || The result of conflating crime reduction with development has been a widening of the police net, in which millions of poor South Africans are caught up every year, with insufficient change in what happens to those caught in it.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques security-driven urban renewal and recommends addressing root causes of crime (socioeconomic development) rather than relying on aggressive policing and containment. It highlights the counterproductive effects of militarized policing on community trust and development.

title: Living Beirut's Security Zones: An Investigation of the Modalities and Practice of Urban Security
thesis: Security in Beirut is fragmented, overlapping, and reflects political divisions, reinforcing social hierarchies and constraining daily urban practices.
key_quotes: These days, I feel that I am back in the village except that those who are harassing me, inquiring about my whereabouts and ordering me around are 100 strangers, dressed in different costumes, playing police... || A certain 'normalization' of security has occurred in the perception of many city dwellers who see security elements as part of the daily hassles they deal with. || Like capital, security has become one more form in which existing social hierarchies are consolidated and/or challenged and new ones imposed.
policy_relevance: None

title: The uneven geographies of the Olympic carceral: from exceptionalism to normalisation
thesis: Olympic security planning creates hyper-carceral spaces that normalise exceptional security measures, producing uneven geographies and transferring military-carceral strategies across host cities.
key_quotes: This again connects with an enduring set of processes by which, slowly but surely, we see military–threat–response technologies and procedures being repurposed for use in the civic realm (Graham 2010). || In such spatial configurations the rule of law is suspended to facilitate extraordinary social control where citizens can be literally stripped of political rights (homo sacer) altering the established relationship between the state/sovereign and the citizenry within a particular territory, most graphically represented by the prisoner camp. || the spatial imprints and uneven geographies of such strategies can be seen to represent a contemporary carceral archipelago where the spaces that are secured, and their social and material effect on adjacent areas, the host city, or the wider nation, are relevant to contemporary urban restructuring debates within geography
policy_relevance: Critiques the normalisation of exceptional security measures in mega-events, highlighting the need for proportionality and the risks of permanent security legacies that exacerbate urban inequalities.

title: Housing as Battleground: Targeting the City in the Battles of Algiers
thesis: During the Algerian War, housing in Algiers was militarized through the state of exception, transforming dwellings into tools of surveillance, control, and resistance.
key_quotes: What has received less attention, however, is the degree to which housing complexes and residential districts also became targets of strategic militarization. || The sudden proliferation of emergency dwellings, like those erected in the Mahieddine and the Clos Salembier, represented a new stage in the militarization of housing in Algiers. || In this context, military officers became self-styled urban theorists as the numerous bidonvilles (shantytowns) in Algiers were placed directly under their control, and new emergency dwelling models––above all the cité de transit––were codified as their weapons of choice.
policy_relevance: The paper discusses the state of emergency as a legal framework enabling militarized urban transformation, and notes its later reapplication in France for rehousing bidonville residents, with implications for contemporary states of emergency.

title: “Homeland” Insecurities? Katrina and the Politics of “Security” in Metropolitan America
thesis: The Bush administration's post-9/11 focus on terrorism undermined urban preparedness for natural disasters like Katrina, revealing the politics of security.
key_quotes: In disturbing echoes of Baghdad and Fallujah, U.S. Army commanders, in response to Katrina, talked openly in the Army Times about the need to launch 'urban combat' operations to 'take back' the city from 'insurgents' who had bred anarchy and violence. || The Katrina disaster unerringly revealed some of the stark politics that surround 'security' in the post-9/11 United States. || Such a policy shift may have directly contributed to the scale and devastation of Katrina. In early 2004, the federal government withdrew moneys from levee maintenance around New Orleans to pay for homeland security programs and the Iraq war budget.
policy_relevance: Critiques the diversion of resources from disaster mitigation to antiterror spending; implies need for balanced security policies that address natural hazards and climate change.

title: From ‘Violence-complacent’ to ‘Terrorist-ready’: Post-9/11 Framing of the US Super Bowl
thesis: Post-9/11 news media framed the Super Bowl as both vulnerable and safe, incorporating these frames into pro-growth discourse to maintain hegemonic ideology and justify militarization of urban space.
key_quotes: The massive security build-up that accompanies the Super Bowl is thus presented as the ‘new normal’. || In post-9/11 era, the Super Bowl is both ‘vulnerable’ and ‘the safest place on earth’. And we are ‘privileged’ host communities and football fans, even as we are surveilled, digitally scanned, corralled, barricaded and patted-down. || Rather than re-place the pro-growth discourse, these frames were effectively incorporated by journalists into the pro-growth discourse—both vulnerability and safety are now presented as contributing to the ‘fact’ that hosting a Super Bowl is good for the city-as-a-whole.
policy_relevance: None explicitly. The paper critiques the militarization of urban space and the acceptance of security measures, but offers no policy recommendations.

title: Privatizing Security, Securitizing Policing: The Case of the G20 in Toronto, Canada
thesis: Examines how the privatization and securitization of policing during the G20 in Toronto blur internal/external security, militarize urban space, and undermine democratic accountability.
key_quotes: Long-range acoustical devices (LRADs), or 'sound cannons,' were originally developed by the US military for use against Somali pirates and Iraqi insurgents, only to be later tested 'at home' in the space of the city during Pittsburgh's 2009 hosting of the G20. || The idea that 'security is coming home' (Coaffee and Wood 2006) shapes cities in particular ways... the 'reciprocal dynamic of urban securitization' or the 'urbanization of security' (Coward 2009:399) in which 'the security agenda is urbanized and urbanity is insofar as it induces insecurity and vulnerability—securitized' has particular implications for cities. || increased militarization is not only fought through the city but is related to what some have called 'urbicide' and a war on cities (Campbell, Graham and Monk 2007; Cowen 2007).
policy_relevance: Recommends repeal of the Public Works Protection Act (later enacted); emphasizes need for public debate on acquisition of military-grade equipment by police; highlights accountability gaps and constitutional concerns with security regulations.

title: Governing the Contested City: Geographies of Displacement in Diyarbakır, Turkey
thesis: Urban renewal projects in Suriçi, as part of a post-conflict urban regime, rendered Kurdish lower-class dwellers displaceable and paved the way for subsequent destruction during urban warfare.
key_quotes: This abrupt shift from renewal schemes aiming to forge a governmental spatio-politics to draconian measures that Öktem (2019) describes as 'urbicide' requires examining the processes that inform the spatiality of politics in the successive conjunctures of non-conflict and conflict. || The idea of securitisation through marketisation has invigorated urban imaginaries that devalue lower-class Kurdish dweller's experience attached to place. The post-conflict rehabilitation has stripped dwellers of their right to the city by depicting their everyday forms of urbanity as unfit. || Displaceability here is crucial to understand how the violence expressed in further re-militarisation of space during and after the urban warfare became possible. As 'the state of being susceptible to involuntary distancing from' urban material and cultural resources and right to the city (Yiftachel 2020:154), displaceability 'holds large parts of urban society in suspense, often living on borrowed time in conditions of growing vulnerability and uncertainty'.
policy_relevance: None

title: Slow urbicide: Accounting for the shifting temporalities of political violence in the West Bank
thesis: The paper proposes 'slow urbicide' to capture the gradual, attritional destruction of Palestinian urbanity in the West Bank through Israeli settlement policies and environmental violence.
key_quotes: The article proposes the concept of 'slow urbicide' to account for the shifting temporalities of urbicidal violence as much as for its reliance on, or activation of, human and more-than-human agencies and forces. || Slow urbicide... involves a gradual destruction of Palestinian urbanity through such strategies as physical strangulation, obscure systems of land administration, bureaucratic neglect, pollution, and obliteration of the vernacular landscape. || The policy of intense, cartographically premeditated settlement in the West Bank... mobilizes one form of urbanity (Israeli) against another (Palestinian) and is deliberately aimed at the suppression of the latter.
policy_relevance: None

title: Atmospheric geographies of (counter)terrorism
geography: Western Europe (with references to UK, France, Germany, Israel/Palestine, Colombia, Lebanon, Indonesia)
thesis: This paper argues for an atmospheric approach to studying everyday urban experiences of (counter)terrorism, focusing on diffuse, felt experiences and the role of crowds and difference.
key_quotes: We argue that thinking atmospherically about the spaces of urban encounters with (counter)terrorism is important, firstly, to identify and question feelings and dispositions shaped by discourses, practices, and infrastructures of (counter)terrorism; secondly, to contribute spatial perspectives of felt experience to literatures on security and (counter)terrorism in geography and beyond; thirdly, to connect official understandings of (counter)terrorism with its everyday felt experiences and materialities. || Counterterrorism is replete with examples of specific policing and practices acting 'beyond the realm of the observable' and becoming embodied at the everyday level [...] that warrant consideration here for their atmospheric aspects and impacts. || How then might different atmospheres come into being through the performance of variously expressive activities amongst such materialities? There are evident parallels here when it comes to such a concern with both the material realities of urban environments and their role in securing people and institutions from the threat of terrorism, and the host of practices of policing and securing that seek to set a certain tone amongst this.
policy_relevance: Discusses UK Protect Duty consultation and EU SafeCi project; highlights the need for policy to engage with diverse publics and the atmospheric/affective impacts of counterterrorism measures, not just physical security.

title: The State, Sewers, and Security: How Does the Egyptian State Reframe Environmental Disasters as Terrorist Threats?
thesis: The Egyptian state reframed the 2015 Alexandria floods as a terrorist attack to entrench repressive rule, obfuscating infrastructural neglect and climate change.
key_quotes: Blaming terrorists for targeting Egypt's urban sanitation infrastructure, however, revealed how the state's narrative of terrorism and security extended into its repressive approach to urban environmental governance. || Terrorism became the master discourse through which the floods were now to be understood; this narrative shifted the urgency of improving environmental governance or infrastructural development to a focus on terrorism's attendant state response, increased security. || I argue that in the current political moment in Egypt and across the globe, the discourse of terrorism and its attendant statist response of security have become important forces in urban environmental governance and infrastructural development.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the use of terrorism discourse to justify securitization and repressive governance, and calls for attention to infrastructural neglect and climate change rather than security responses.

title: Security Zones and New York City's Shrinking Public Space
thesis: This paper empirically measures the extent of security zones in Lower Manhattan, finding that 27% of non-building area is now secured, and argues this new land use shrinks public space and threatens democratic urban life.
key_quotes: We argue that this new type of land use is an important and permanent feature of twenty-first century global cities. || Public spaces are the lifeblood of cities. More than simple physical entities, truly public spaces are sites of interaction in which individuals are sometimes forced to interact with those whom they usually criticize or dislike. || The diminution of the public realm was palpable in both neighborhoods: clearly, the security zone is a new type of land use and deserves more earnest consideration by the planning and development community.
policy_relevance: The paper recommends that cities inventory their public realm, balance security with openness, and consider more flexible security measures. It notes that pedestrianization for security purposes might be politically palatable.

title: 21 Militarized Civic Ritual: Pentagon, Police, and US Professional Football
thesis: Militarized civic rituals, exemplified by the NFL's relationship with the US military and homeland security, have become routine in US cities, blurring civilian-military boundaries and legally equating fans with citizen-soldiers.
key_quotes: In this chapter I suggest that militarized civic rituals have now become an ever-present feature of US urban life and represent a troubling new conflation between military and civilian discourses and practices employed through sport, particularly the NFL and the Super Bowl. || This effectively means that the NFL is legally viewed the same as a Pentagon supplier, and the fans in attendance, and the citizens in the urban spaces, are the soldiers at war. || Legally equated with a soldier at war, the NFL fan's call of duty is perceived through a mobile phone application, everyday citizens recruited to assist, in the name of patriotism, in terrorism prevention. This blurs legal and operational separations between intelligence-gathering and citizenship and further collapses civilian-military boundaries suggesting a changed notion of duty for all US residents.
policy_relevance: Discusses the SAFETY Act (2002) which provides liability protection to anti-terrorism technology sellers, including the NFL, and the Government Contractor Defense that immunizes sellers against claims from terrorist acts; notes that citizens are not informed of their legal status as soldiers and lack the benefits (e.g., veteran pensions, medical care) that actual soldiers receive; recommends awareness of militarization and its implications for citizenship.

title: An Intelligent Surveillance Platform for Large Metropolitan Areas with Dense Sensor Deployment
thesis: A technical description of an intelligent video surveillance platform using low-cost sensors and multiple AI engines for autonomous alarm detection in urban environments.
key_quotes: This paper presents an intelligent surveillance platform based on the usage of large numbers of inexpensive sensors designed and developed inside the European Eureka Celtic project HuSIMS. || The fact that the system is using low resolution visual sensors provides an additional advantage regarding governance and politics: the provided image does not usually allow recognition of people’s faces, which makes the system more respectful of privacy. || HuSIMS' main target is to provide real-time alerts for irregular activity in both indoors and outdoors scenarios.
policy_relevance: None

title: Competitive Cities and Secure Nations: Conflict and Convergence in Urban Waterfront Agendas after 9/11
thesis: Post-9/11 port security and competitive city waterfront redevelopment agendas are both conflicting and converging, with implications for social justice.
key_quotes: While proponents of competitive city projects appear directly concerned with promoting a particular vision of capitalist urban development in contrast to the national security agenda of port and border securitization, we contend that a simple dichotomy between 'economy' and 'security' cannot capture their complex intermingling. || The securitization of urban ports against potential terrorism in the US is imagined by government officials and security strategists as a front-line strategy in the protection of goods that flow into national transportation systems. || Whether urban waterfronts are rebuilt and policed in the interests of national security, local property developers and professional condominium residents, or all of these simultaneously, a large proportion of urban citizens are not a part of that picture.
policy_relevance: The paper highlights the exclusionary implications of the convergence of security and economic agendas for marginalized groups, emphasizing the need for attention to spatial justice in waterfront cities.

title: Future war in cities: Urbanization's challenge to strategic studies in the 21st century
thesis: Western militaries must engage with urban studies to develop nuanced strategies for diverse urban environments, moving beyond a narrow focus on megacities.
key_quotes: One of the continuing weaknesses of Western strategic studies is the paucity of serious research on the role of the city in armed conflict. || Because cities represent crucibles of civilization, it is uncomfortable to regard them as arenas for future armed conflict or as scenes of humanitarian emergency. || In the coming years, if we are to better understand the city as an armed conflict zone, an urban-oriented strand of strategic studies needs to be developed by security scholars working in close conjunction with the macro- and micro-level schools identified earlier.
policy_relevance: Recommends developing an urban-oriented strategic studies, engaging with urban specialists, and using discriminate force to reduce civilian casualties and uphold humanitarian law.

title: Urban resilience and national security: the role for planning
geography: UK, with references to USA, Israel/Palestine, Northern Ireland
thesis: This paper analyzes how counter-terrorism urban resilience has become embedded in planning, shifting from crude militaristic fortification to a more integrated role for built environment professionals, raising concerns about proportionality and co-option.
key_quotes: 'blast resistant design specialists and the tools they use to understand explosions are Cold War legacies...such specialists were deployed to defend not civilian buildings, but military facilities such as missile silos or bunkers. Now, however, in response to the threat of terrorist attack against civil buildings, civil planners are being urged to incorporate resilience for counter-terrorism.' (para 3.2) || 'The link between the military and planning in Israel must be viewed not only in a historical context but also in terms of different strategies of intervention at national, regional and local scales creating a 'security scape' preoccupied with 'impending threats, defence strategies and precautionary measures'.' (para 3.1) || 'The truth is we do not design buildings to withstand bomb blasts because bomb blasts are the exception to the rule…the key point is the defining of the line between risk and recklessness.' (para 3.2, quoting Finch 1996)
policy_relevance: Discusses UK policy implications: Contest strategy, National Security Strategy, need for planning training, integration of counter-terrorism into building design, tension between proportionality and over-reaction, and potential for co-option of planning profession into security agenda.

title: Violence and domestic space: demolition and destruction of homes in the occupied Palestinian territories
geography: occupied Palestinian territories (West Bank, East Jerusalem, Gaza)
thesis: Examines systematic demolition of Palestinian homes as violence, dispossession, and ethnic cleansing, using planning and military tactics to control urban space.
key_quotes: In that demolition I lost everything. I lost all the memories of my life—pictures, documents, belongings from my childhood, my wedding, our years in Saudi Arabia. Everything that meant something to me personally. We lost all our possessions—our furniture, appliances. All our savings from all those years of work were gone. || Israel has turned urban planning into a tool of the government, to be used to help prevent the expansion of the city's non-Jewish population. In East Jerusalem in particular, it is a way of limiting the number of new homes built in Arab neighbourhoods, and thereby ensuring that the Arab percentage of the city's population—28.8% in 1967—does not grow beyond this level. || The most disturbing thing to me is that there is an absolutely wild west in the occupied territories. Brigade Commanders, Regiment Commanders and Company Commanders do whatever comes to their minds. No one checks them, and no one stops them.
policy_relevance: Calls for an end to house demolitions and occupation; highlights the need for international pressure and recognition of planning as a tool of dispossession.

title: The geo-historical legacies of urban security governance and the Vancouver 2010 Olympics
thesis: Mega-events like the Olympics catalyse long-term militarisation of urban policing through joint training and jurisdictional blurring, as seen in the Vancouver Police Department's Military Liaison Unit.
key_quotes: The paper furthers Stephen Graham’s (2010) New Military Urbanism that considers the circulation of military expertise between neo-colonial frontiers of military intervention with Western urban spaces. || In this way, models of ‘pacification’, ‘militarisation’ and ‘control’, as the practical means through which the West prosecutes its military interventions, are remerging in Western urban contexts through a ‘boomerang effect’. || The MLU has trained members who are currently serving in Afghanistan and Sudan, demonstrating how the military police model is applicable to their own geo-political operations.
policy_relevance: The paper highlights under-recognised security legacies of mega-events and calls for empirical attention to institutional-level geographies of policing and militarisation.

title: Spatial Alternatives and Counter-Sovereignties in Israel/Palestine
thesis: Explores how micro-level spatial alternatives and counter-sovereignties can challenge hyper-securitized spatial logics and foster nonviolent overlapment in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.
key_quotes: Graham (2004) distinguishes Israeli construction (for example, new settlements, barriers, and roads) with the de-construction of the urban and infrastructural assets of the Palestinians (demolishing houses, for example), labeled 'urbicide.' || Sari Hanafi (2005) terms the destruction of the full spectrum of Palestinian life—erased from the land—as 'spacio-cide.' || Weizman (2004) and Weizman and Lein (2002) focus on the developmental aspect of Israel's strategy in the Occupied Territories. They argue that the Israeli strategy in the Occupied Territories centers on three-dimensional control over the totality of space: infrastructure, the environment, and sub- and above-surface domains—a combination which orchestrates a 'politics of verticality' using planning and architecture.
policy_relevance: Suggests rethinking sovereignty through fragmented, counter-, and social sovereignties at micro and local scales; advocates for shared governance of contested sites like Temple Mount/Haram al-Sharif via community-based authorities; notes potential of civil society activism and everyday practices to create spaces of nonviolent overlapment.

title: The Emergence of a Military Urban in and of War
thesis: Traces the historical-conceptual emergence of a 'military urban' in U.S. military practice, where the urban becomes a distinct object of knowledge and management, enabling new forms of military action.
key_quotes: a gradual shift has occurred in terms of how the armed forces have begun to think of and act on the urban as a distinct object that can be made “known” and managed in and through a specialized knowledge. || The entire urban environment must be addressed simultaneously and systematically by applying power to disable hostile elements and enable those environmental elements that are essential to the city’s functioning. || just as a living organism relies on flows (in food, air and water), and flows out (waste) to stay alive, a city also requires flows
policy_relevance: None explicitly; offers critical understanding of military epistemology and its weaponization of knowledge for urban warfare.

title: The Intimate Entrenchment of Philadelphia's Drug War
thesis: The drug war in Philadelphia's inner city is maintained through militarized discourse and practices, but residents resist by occupying and defending the block as intimate spaces of survival and community.
key_quotes: Through the military transfer programme implemented by congress in the 1990s, the PPD has a weapons arsenal supplied directly by the armed forces. In April 2013, there was a brief scandal when the PPD lost an M-16 assault rifle... Department officials noted that they were in possession of 1355 M-16 assault rifles in their arsenal. The weapons were given to the department by the US army.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the militarized approach to drug enforcement and suggests that policy should recognize the importance of semi-public spaces for residents' survival and community, rather than treating them solely as front lines of a war.

title: Walking Through Walls: The Invisible War
thesis: The Israeli 'walking through walls' strategy during the 2002 invasion of Nablus constitutes urban warfare that destroys domestic space and suspends everyday life, while inhabitants develop 'making-do' tactics to resist and cope.
key_quotes: The Israeli assault and the 'walking through walls' mark a twofold military strategy. On one hand, it undermines the already slow modernization of the Palestinian urban society; ... On the other hand, it is of deliberate urban destruction that is closely integrated with Israeli's overall colonization efforts through carefully planned construction of place and space as a broader strategy of annihilation of the Palestinian landscape (Graham, 2004). || The 'walking through walls' not only turned inside space into outside space and the private domain to the thoroughfare, but also transformed the meaning of everyday space into a 'forbidden space' where it became a medium of warfare. || This article signifies that warfare, like everything else, is being urbanized and cities are the key sites: 'War has entered the city again—the sphere of the everyday, the private realm of the house' (Misselwitz & Weizman, 2003, p. 272; cf. Graham, 2004).
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that planning in conflict zones should incorporate the lived experience and 'making-do' tactics of inhabitants, but does not provide specific policy recommendations.

title: Violent infrastructure, nationalist stigmatisation and spatial erasure
thesis: Turkish nationalist infrastructure in Diyarbakir inflicts symbolic violence by stigmatizing and erasing Kurdish identity, but Kurdish residents also resist and reaffirm their identity through the same space.
key_quotes: In general, urban infrastructure is a mechanism of state power. But, through the case of the imposing presence of Turkish nationalist infrastructure in the Kurdish city Diyarbakir, it demonstrates that when tied to an antagonistic nationalist political project, this infrastructure is often purposefully built to violently cleanse urban spaces of the national 'other'. || Statues, murals and slogans cannot injure, maim or kill. So, the Turkish infrastructure in Dağkapı Square does not result in any physical violence. Instead, my interlocutors' experiences reveal that it inflicts a form of symbolic violence as the infrastructure works to stigmatise and erase their Kurdish identity. || That is not abnormal. Remember how I used to be beaten up in school for speaking Kurdish? Before that I spoke Kurdish, but I never knew that I was Kurdish. But when I was beaten up I really understood that I was Kurdish, I felt Kurdish, and I wanted to say, 'I am Kurdish'. When we lined up for lunch the teacher would say, Ne mutlu Türküm diyene. But we would whisper to each other Ne mutlu Kürdüm diyene.
policy_relevance: None

title: The war on teenage terrorists: Philly's 'Flash Mob Riots' and the banality of post-9/11 securitization
thesis: Philadelphia's response to gatherings of African American youth as 'flash mobs' uses banal post-9/11 antiterrorism discourse to justify aggressive policing and reinforce historical racial and class segregation.
key_quotes: This paper interprets a recent, aggressive state crackdown on public gatherings of African American youth in the streets of Philadelphia's commercial districts against the backdrop of historical geographies of race and disinvestment. Drawing on news accounts and government publications, and deploying theories of securitization and space, it joins those who argue that the performance of security in everyday spaces works to conceal the social relations undergirding the post-9/11 security state. We consider how city officials and others have constructed the collective figure of the 'flash mob' as a perpetrator of urban terrorism and the subject of state intervention.
policy_relevance: Critiques the use of antiterrorism legislation and surveillance to preempt youth gatherings and curtail civil rights, calling for closer attention to the social warrant of racialized space and banal terrorism.

title: Suspicious cities: An analysis of the securitisation of urban everyday life in London and Brussels
thesis: Urban everyday life in London and Brussels has been incrementally securitised under counterterrorism, with human and non-human bodies increasingly assigned suspiciousness, constituting a process of urban segregation with ethical implications for collective responsibility.
key_quotes: I conceptualise urban everyday life as an entanglement of intra-acting sites, objects, and people. || the securitisation of everyday life in European metropoles constitutes a process of urban segregation. || everyone and everything that intra-acts in urban everyday life is also to some extent responsible for its securitisation
policy_relevance: Calls for critical reflection and resistance to securitisation, but no specific policy recommendations.

title: Walls and shadows: The occupation of Baghdad
thesis: The occupation of Baghdad created a segregated, dual city of walls and shadows, where American military control and isolation fostered violence, racism, and failure.
key_quotes: The paper examines the complex dynamics of urban occupation from the author's particular vantage, exploring how technology, doctrine, psychology, and tactics interrelate in the high-stress combat environment. Drawing wider conclusions from his experience, the author argues that the occupation of Baghdad offers a bleak vision of our urban future, a future where security for the few promotes a violent anarchy for the many, a future of walls and the shadows they cast. || The overall system comprised a dispersal of fortress-like FOBs, each surrounded by enormous concrete barriers and guarded by watchtowers manned by machine-gun crews, connected by routes running along the major expressways, which themselves hosted military convoys, patrols and checkpoints, all forming a lattice of American quasi-control laid over the teeming metropolis of Baghdad like a second city, an American network deliberately separate from, bypassing and avoiding as much of the real city as possible. || That is, going outside the wire, leaving the FOB, was not just to enter into a city full of hostile people, but it was to enter a city that was, in itself, hostile, that was, in its very roads and sidewalks, the enemy. It was as if Baghdad itself was trying to kill us.
policy_relevance: None, but the paper implies that militarized segregation and lack of cultural engagement are counterproductive.

title: The Applicability of International Humanitarian Law in Peacetime Urban Civilian Operations: Analysing the Deployment of the Army to Fight Gang Violence in the Cape Flats
thesis: Analyses whether the military deployment against Cape Flats gang violence is justified under IHL, concluding the violence is an 'other situation of violence' not triggering armed conflict law.
key_quotes: The situation of gang violence in Cape Town cannot be classified as urban warfare. ... it is not a military operation, but the main proponents and victims are civilians. || Stupart argues that the army is not well suited for combating gangsterism in Cape Town because soldiers are trained to 'find, fix and finish' their 'enemy'. ... gang members are not distinguishable from civilians. || The Cape Flats comprise of purpose-built ghettos with no communal amenities and no employment opportunities either. These new settlements were designed in such a way as to limit the number of points of exit and entry, in a bid to ensure that the inhabitants could easily be policed and cordoned off by the apartheid government.
policy_relevance: Implies that a multi-pronged socio-economic approach is needed rather than military intervention; highlights the politicisation of gang violence as a barrier to effective policy.

title: In dangerous times: War, reconstruction and the city
geography: global, with focus on Middle East (Lebanon, Syria, Palestine, Iraq, Gaza, Yugoslavia)
thesis: The article argues that urban destruction and reconstruction are linked through a post-conflict-catastrophe complex that reinforces neocolonial relations, militarism, and neoliberal marketization.
key_quotes: The central argument: cities today are both productive of and produced by scale-jumping flows of people, ideas, goods, finance, technology, and aesthetic practices, all mediated by complex assemblages of institutions and regulation, above, below and shooting through, the state. (p. 205) || What some call urbicide (Graham 2004, 2011), however, is most devastatingly visible in contemporary late-modern warfare (Belcher 2011), itself a product of global transformations that fragment states and give rise to a range of sub-state political and military forces. (p. 205) || Israel's use of two such systems, known as Lavender and Where's Daddy?, may be indicative of what's to come. These systems are used to create kill lists of suspected Hamas fighters and 'operatives' down to the lowest levels. These suspects are targeted not in battle, but often tracked to their homes, where they are killed along with their families, often multiple generations at a time (Abraham 2024; Tharoor 2024). Without meaningful human oversight, and combined with the unprecedented destructive power of today's weapons, contemporary urban warfare gives lie to technophilic dreams of the sanitary smart bomb. (p. 206)
policy_relevance: The article critiques the Post-Conflict/Catastrophe Complex (P3C) and its neoliberal reconstruction policies, calling for anthropological engagement with alternative paths that prioritize local agency, peace, security, and sustainable economic revival over market-driven approaches. It advocates for critical voices to engage 'war where it is made' (p. 207).

title: Predictive Policing: Review of Benefits and Drawbacks
thesis: Predictive policing lacks a clear evidence base; claimed benefits and drawbacks are not empirically supported.
key_quotes: Predictive policing is the collection and analysis of data about previous crimes for identification and statistical prediction of individuals or geospatial areas with an increased probability of criminal activity to help developing policing intervention and prevention strategies and tactics. || The risk here is that predictive policing could result in less effective and maybe even discriminatory police interventions. || We conclude that the current thrust of predictive policing initiatives is based on convincing arguments and anecdotal evidence rather than on systematic empirical research.
policy_relevance: Urges independent empirical testing of both benefits and drawbacks to build an evidence base for predictive policing.

title: Is Big Data challenging criminology?
thesis: Big Data and predictive policing challenge traditional criminology by sidelining theory and causation in favour of correlation, but this approach has serious limitations.
key_quotes: The disregard of theory means that a lot of Big Data analysis (like the random forest algorithm described above) will be regarded as a 'black box'. As Brennan and Oliver (2013: 558) state, 'their logic can be inscrutable to human users … This failure to offer explanatory tools might be awkward for decision makers who must provide justifications for their decisions (e.g., judges, probation officers, and parole boards).' || Because these techniques make predictions with seeming clairvoyance based on methods that people who rely on those predictions cannot understand, there is an 'aura' around the predictions. There are no opportunities to challenge claims about future behaviour based on particular alleged correlations (e.g. race and crime) as they remain hidden. || If there are initial biases in the crimes noticed by police (for example racial bias affecting initial patrolling patterns), then this will be fed back into the algorithm and 'confirm' police biases (see Pasquale, 2015: 39–42). This feedback effect is self-perpetuating, thus unable to be solved by regular updating.
policy_relevance: Discusses implications for predictive policing and criminal justice decisions, urging that decisions require causal understanding, transparency, and evaluation through experiments or quasi-experiments.

title: Predictive Policing and the Politics of Patterns
geography: Norway, Germany, Switzerland, Europe, United States, Australia
thesis: Patterns are the epistemological core of predictive policing, but they vary in rationalities and conceal assumptions, making them political.
key_quotes: Patterns are the epistemological core of predictive policing. With the move towards digital prediction tools, the authority of the pattern is rearticulated and reinforced in police work. || The clean surface of the pattern makes it impossible to defend oneself against their results. || Unless patterns are accompanied and contextualized by explanatory material, they render policing decisions opaque.
policy_relevance: The paper calls for greater transparency and reflection on pattern-based policing, suggesting that patterns should be accompanied by explanatory material to allow police officers and affected citizens to interrogate the assumptions behind predictions.

title: Data Matters: The Politics and Practices of Digital Border and Migration Management
thesis: This introduction argues that data in border and migration management must be studied as matters of concern, knowledge production, and material infrastructure to understand their performative and political effects.
key_quotes: What he describes as the constitution of the 'multipurpose drone' indeed speaks closely to specific modes of seeing, knowing, and acting that become pre-structured through the interaction between human actors, technology, and data. For Loukinas, the alleged 'versatility' of drone technology can thus be mobilised as an analytical lens to reconstruct how diverging types of knowledge and ensuing action can be constituted from a single body of data, depending on the specific relations that data form with their surroundings. || When complex, mutable algorithms analyse large amounts of data, the ways in which recommendations for specific actions (e.g., let this person pass; single out and further question that person) come into being can become difficult or even impossible to understand (Amoore 2011; Côté-Boucher 2010; Leese 2014). A lack of insight into analytical processes in turn undercuts the possibility to challenge and contest decisions. || Data are increasingly used as evidence that supports or falsifies claims made by travellers or asylum seekers. Whereas such claims would in the past need to be manually investigated and their acceptance or rejection would be left to the discretion of border guards or bureaucrats (Magalhães 2018), data are now considered to be telling an unquestionable truth.
policy_relevance: The paper calls for empirical engagement with data practices and infrastructures to expose power asymmetries and contest depoliticizing technocratic language. It suggests that scholars should 'stay with the trouble' and treat data as matters of concern to open them up for political debate and intervention.

title: Beyond data as representation: The performativity of Big Data in surveillance
thesis: Data-based surveillance produces suspect subjectivities parasitically on other data-based subjectivations, requiring a performative rather than representationalist account.
key_quotes: Surveillance is not a separate application of Big Data but a potential that emerges from all uses of data analysis. || The performativity of data in surveillance is parasitical to such other performatives. Thus, no data remains innocent: All ways in which we can become a subject also are ways to become a suspect. || Data-based surveillance is legitimized by the circumspect collection of data which are then put into new relations. It is based on the power relations that emanate by the possibility to cite a wide range of data in contexts of effective authority and governance.
policy_relevance: None

title: Big Data, urban governance, and the ontological politics of hyperindividualism
geography: USA (New York City, Camden, New Jersey)
thesis: Big Data's ontology of hyperindividualism reduces governance to management of atomistic behavior, undermines urban complexity, erodes democracy, and eviscerates collective resistance.
key_quotes: The practice of Big Data governed by an ontology of hyperindividualism is also constitutive of that ontology, naturalizing and diffusing it through practices of governance and, from there, throughout myriad dimensions of everyday life. || Big Data’s hyperindividuated ontology extracts and displaces the data point—the ‘thing’—from the coconstitutive, relational ontology of the assemblage. || Big Data’s ontology of hyperindividualism reduces governance to the management of atomistic behavior, undermines the contribution of urban complexity as a resource for governance, erodes the potential for urban democracy, and eviscerates the possibility of collective resistance.
policy_relevance: Calls for critical reflection on Big Data's ontological assumptions in governance; no specific policy recommendations.

title: Epistemologies of predictive policing: Mathematical social science, social physics and machine learning
thesis: Distinguishes three epistemologies of predictive policing and analyzes their implications for the constitution of predictive knowledge.
key_quotes: "The same approach that lenders use to prequalify potential loan applicants can be used to assess the risk for escalation in a series of burglaries, while the models used to classify shopping patterns and purchasing decisions can be used to identify the motive in a homicide or predict the next incident in a crime series" (McCue and Parker, 2003: 115). || "For ML-based modelling to make explicit the causal mechanisms behind predicted outcomes is of no relevance: 'Understanding a phenomena may lead to improved forecasting accuracy, or it may not, but forecasting and explanation are different enterprises that can work at cross-purposes'" (Berk and Bleich, 2013: 516). || "SP-based and ML-based approaches lead to a lack of algorithmic accountability through a lack of model interpretability"
policy_relevance: None

title: Educating the smart city: Schooling smart citizens through computational urbanism
thesis: Education is being reconfigured as a laboratory for smart city governance, where schools become data platforms and students are trained as computational operatives.
key_quotes: The article contributes two original lines of critical analysis: (1) by tracing how commercial vendors such as IBM and Microsoft are extending their global smart cities programs into a reimagining and reconfiguration of schools as data-based sites of real-time monitoring and measurement, where students are increasingly treated as 'data objects' whose actions can be altered through programming the environment; and (2) by examining how governmental and civil society organizations are working within local smart cities initiatives to develop young people's capacities as active 'smart citizens', with the technical data skills to contribute to computational urbanism by participating in 'civic coding' on behalf of the city. || The programmable environments of the smart city are infused with the aspiration to orchestrate particular urban processes and ways of life through computational logics of programming. The standards that regulate smart cities developments are transcoded into software instruments that then alter the environment and consequently shape the everyday living of urban citizens. || The smart school is a laboratory for experimental forms of digital government where the sociotechnical imaginaries and expertise of computational urbanists and civic coders are to be projected from a distance into the city, both through monitoring young people's data points and through educating them to become active and responsible citizens with appropriate skills to compute the future of the city.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the technocratic and depoliticized nature of smart city education initiatives, highlighting the need for critical engagement with the governance implications of data-driven schooling and the production of 'smart citizens'.

title: Data-Driven Participation: Algorithms, Cities, Citizens, and Corporate Control
thesis: Data-driven civic participation via VGI and algorithms enacts passive engagement, shifts control to corporations, and undermines democratic deliberation.
key_quotes: These repurposed contributions present the public as data—without the need of 'distracting' people from their daily lives in order to actively engage with political activities (Cardone et al., 2013, 2014). || Deconstructing the black boxes of Big Data isn't easy. Even if they were willing to expose their methods to the public, the modern Internet and banking sectors pose tough challenges to our understanding of those methods. The conclusions they come to—about the productivity of employees, or the relevance of websites, or the attractiveness of investments—are determined by complex formulas devised by legions of engineers and guarded by a phalanx of lawyers. (Pasquale, 2015, p. 6) || Data-driven participation consequently shifts from its primary purposes in cases such as PPGIS and active deliberation methods that seek to empower citizens and influence government decision-making. Instead, datafication of participation via VGI propels the integral process of democracy into data-market economies that are largely driven by corporate interests outside those held by government officials and citizens.
policy_relevance: Warns against adopting technological solutions to the 'messiness of democracy' that operate behind coded-doors; calls for examining whether passive data-driven participation signals a decline in more collective and demanding modes of engagement.

title: A spatio-temporal method for crime prediction using historical crime data and transitional zones identified from nightlight imagery
thesis: Proposes a spatio-temporal Cokriging algorithm integrating historical crime data and urban transitional zones (from nightlight imagery) to improve crime prediction accuracy in Cincinnati.
policy_relevance: None

title: Reframing, Reimagining and Remaking Smart Cities
thesis: Smart city initiatives need to be reframed, reimagined and remade through normative, conceptual, practical and political interventions to create more equitable and just urban futures.
key_quotes: In control regimes, people become subject to constant modulation through software-mediated systems in which their behaviour is directed explicitly or implicitly reshaped, rather than being (self)disciplined. || The smart city thus produces a particular form of governmentality, what Vanolo (2014) terms 'smartmentality'. || Far from being impartial and objective, smart city technologies have built-in normative values and judgements about how systems should perform, and how they assess and manage outcomes, with these hardcoded into the underlying software.
policy_relevance: The chapter recommends a multi-pronged approach to privacy and security including market-driven, technological, policy/regulatory/legal, and governance/management solutions, and advocates for co-creation and co-production between stakeholders.

title: Policing the future, disrupting urban policy today. Predictive policing, smart city, and urban policy in Memphis (TN)
thesis: 通过实证批判孟菲斯Blue CRUSH预测性警务，揭示其缺乏预防犯罪效力，并证明它通过促进治安扩张、破坏警察工作而重塑城市政策，从而批判智慧城市的救世话语。
key_quotes: the article, first, shows that there is no evidence of Blue CRUSH's capacity to prevent crime, thus adding empirical material to skepticism over the role of predictive policing as a policy solution in the first place. And, second, it argues that, rather than making crime a matter of technological solutions, predictive policing shifts the politics therein – in short, it contributes to the expansion of policing into the field of urban policy at the same time as it disrupts present police work. || The smart city, in this sense, can be understood as the ultimate attempt at deploying technology as ideology, an ideology that is typical of the neoliberal(izing) city: the corporatization of urban services, dismantling of welfare programs, and over-securitization of public space. || the collection of massive data about crime raises problems of privacy and data handling, particularly when data are shared among governmental agencies and corporations. Third, predictive policing is heavily shaped by the data it uses; and in contexts where enforcement, hence reporting, is influenced by class and racial biases (the USA being the quintessentially problematic case), it cannot help but reproduce those same biases through its algorithmic elaboration.
policy_relevance: 论文指出预测性警务将资源从社会政策转向治安，加剧紧缩和不平等，并呼吁超越技术解决方案，追求更公正的城市治理。

title: AI audits for assessing design logics and building ethical systems: the case of predictive policing algorithms
thesis: AI audits should evaluate the theoretical foundations of algorithms to uncover hidden biases and avoid harms, using predictive policing as a case example.
key_quotes: the inner workings of black box systems particularly ML models can become opaque, making it difficult to anticipate, understand and mitigate risks. || PPAs can have self-reinforcing properties fuelled by their underpinning near repeat/SEPPs design. Systematics in the models generate feedback loops that repeatedly target the same areas || audits should investigate and question typically less visible dimensions, such as the theoretical assumptions about human behaviour and the social world, that can infuse tech design with potential social implications.
policy_relevance: Recommends that AI audits evaluate theoretical foundations; suggests questions for auditors to uncover design logics; advocates for design justice to diversify AI development.

title: The Making of Crime Predictions: Sociotechnical Assemblages and the Controversies of Governing Future Crime
thesis: Traces the sociotechnical assemblage of CrimeRadar to show how political choices and biases are embedded in algorithmic crime forecasts, challenging claims of objectivity.
key_quotes: As often happens with big data and machine-learning innovations, automated decisions with deep influence in society are made by algorithms hidden in black boxes (Pasquale 2015). || the algorithm itself is powered by 'concrete data, and its mathematics has no bias.... If a crime happened, the algorithm will see it, will read it without putting human values, and will make a prediction based on that. So, it's certainly impartial'. || the multiple choices involved in these practices are naturalized and de-politicized in the process of translating crime events into strings of codes, datasets, and maps.
policy_relevance: None

title: Digitalising Asylum Procedures: The Legitimisation of Smartphone Data Extraction for Retrospective Border Control
thesis: Examines how smartphone data extraction became a legitimate policy instrument in asylum procedures through moralising securitisation and techno-solutionist rationalisations.
key_quotes: The re-appropriation of this everyday technology for purposes of border control marks a critical innovation in digital infrastructures in this sphere. || the use of computers as intermediaries is linked to conceptions of machine-to-machine communication as a legally and socio-politically unproblematic process. || a metadata discourse produces notions of objective and apolitical machine-based outcomes.
policy_relevance: Discusses implications for liberal democratic governance, privacy, data protection, and procedural safeguards. Notes German Federal Administrative Court ruling requiring changes to SDE practice. Highlights need for balancing security and rights in digital border control.

title: Exploitation as innovation: research ethics and the governance of experimentation in the urban living lab
thesis: Urban living labs that experiment on people using data technologies should be governed by research ethics frameworks to address exploitation and power asymmetries.
key_quotes: This paper argues that instances where people themselves are the subjects of the experiment, rather than the technology, suggest that we need to have options for regulating such experimentation. || The kind of lab analysed in this paper instead experiments on people, using technology. || As urban experimentation becomes simultaneously more prevalent and less visible to the public, research ethics can help us ask what kind of power is being exerted through experimentation, and what avenues of resistance may be available to experimental subjects.
policy_relevance: The paper recommends that city authorities impose research ethics frameworks on living labs, including independent auditing, clear contractual agreements, sunset clauses, and enforcement of rules to prevent exploitation and protect residents' autonomy and dignity.

title: Correlated impulses: Using Facebook interests to improve predictions of crime rates in urban areas
geography: United States (Baltimore, Boston, Chicago, Dallas, Los Angeles, New York, Philadelphia, San Francisco, Washington)
thesis: Facebook interests can improve predictions of crime rates in urban areas beyond demographic factors.
key_quotes: The Facebook algorithms that generate the data are a black box, creating two issues. The first is one of substantive interpretation and what exactly it means for a particular ZIP code to be high in a given interest. The second is that changes in these algorithms would mean that the models need to be re-calibrated over time for long-term prediction purposes. || Last, there is a general caveat for modern digital data resources: 'researcher beware' [40–42]. || This study is exploratory, thus we propose no a priori hypotheses linking particular preferences to a given theory of criminality.
policy_relevance: None

title: Data Corruption: The Institutional Cultures of Data Collection and the Case of a Crime-Mapping System in Latin America
thesis: This study examines how institutional cultures and police officers' data practices corrupt crime data in a crime-mapping system, revealing the politics of data-driven policing in the Global South.
key_quotes: The data produced to track crime are also used to inform performance outcome measures. When agents of surveillance are exposed to surveillance themselves, their attitude toward work and the tracking system changes. || It is important to take into consideration that urban crime data are actually used for several other purposes beyond policing, including the governing of cities at other levels: public policymaking, local planning, the allocation of public budgets, and investment in communities impacted by crime. || From the perspective of the Global South, this case study calls attention to the need for developing accounts of how institutional agents operationalize data in organizational cultures and social contexts characterized by pervasive corruption and inequality.
policy_relevance: Calls for data justice, accountability in data production, and critical data studies from the Global South; notes limitations of open data approaches.

title: DATA-DRIVEN CRIMINAL JUSTICE IN THE AGE OF ALGORITHMS: EPISTEMIC CHALLENGES AND PRACTICAL IMPLICATIONS
