thesis: Argues for prioritizing theory- and causation-based algorithms over opaque correlational ones in criminal justice, while critically using the latter with abductive reasoning.
key_quotes: the measured usage of theory and causation-based algorithms is preferable over correlational (i.e., causally opaque) algorithms as support tools in the penal system. || the normative debate on these tools cannot be separated from their epistemic and scientific description without reducing their evaluation ad absurdum. || the epistemological value that can be attributed to correlations and predictions in general
policy_relevance: Discusses the need for standards for trustworthy algorithms (e.g., EU AI HLEG Assessment List) and advocates for incorporating epistemological considerations into the design and evaluation of algorithmic tools in criminal justice.

title: Big Data applied to criminal investigations: expectations of professionals of police cooperation in the European Union
thesis: Explores expectations of EU police cooperation professionals regarding Big Data in criminal investigations using DNA databases, highlighting perceived benefits (cold cases, interoperability) and risks (genetic discrimination, privacy).
key_quotes: I think this project [Big Data] is worked in EUROPOL, according to what I heard. They are doing something like this [Big Data], to connect all the information from the police which is about criminal acts (...) I think this is an analytical weapon (...) to connect all of this information and to put it into some sort of sheet, it is now an analytical sheet, just to complete also with forensic, biological and photography, fingerprint, DNA. And this [Big Data] could be very helpful in these cases. || This is an ethical question. The [Big Data] analysis, we could have bad profiling. We do not want bad profiling. Because you could find that people with certain loci are more criminals, there are more criminals in a certain… But this correlation could not be a real correlation. (...) My opinion is that we have to analyse those kind of connections, but we could be very careful with this. || Well, if I have something to hide, I would not want it [Big Data]. But being the normal law-abiding citizen, I do not have any problem with that. I cannot see anyone having any problem unless you have something to hide. (...) So, OK, maybe my privacy is not going to be as private, but if something happens to my property, thanks to the system it [Big Data] can help me, for example, to apprehend the suspect or perpetrator.
policy_relevance: Highlights the need for regulation and data protection frameworks for Big Data in criminal investigations, and calls for anticipatory governance to address transparency, accountability, and public trust.

title: Pandemic surveillance and mobilities across Sydney, New South Wales
thesis: The paper argues that COVID-19 surveillance in Sydney deepened uneven sensory power, leaving lasting scars in Western Sydney despite dismantling of overt tools.
key_quotes: We argue that these technologies are examples of sensory power which rapidly enrolled human bodies in systems of surveillance that were difficult to unravel through 2022 and beyond. || the idea of 'back to normal' is troubled by the experiences of lockdowns and policing of mobilities in different parts of Sydney. || as the response to the crisis unfolds there is a need for geographers and others to document the ways in which a new surveillance and biopolitical regime is being produced through the alliance of government control and surveillance capitalism and their use of a range of technologies.
policy_relevance: None explicit, but highlights the need for equitable crisis response and awareness of lasting community impacts.

title: The Canadian Clearview AI Investigation as a Call for Digital Policy Literacy
thesis: Argues that digital policy literacy (DPL) is needed to critically understand privacy issues from Clearview AI, moving beyond individualist approaches to privacy.
key_quotes: Rob Kitchin (2014: 2) has argued, big data thus involves new epistemologies where 'rather than testing a theory by analysing relevant data, new data analytics seek to gain insights 'born from the data.'' || biometric identification technologies such as facial recognition software can enact significant harms in their inherent misidentifications || the solutions proposed to deal with these problems reflect a narrow version of digital literacy that would benefit from the expanded concerns of the DPL model
policy_relevance: Calls for stronger privacy laws, regulatory reform (Bill C-27), and a digital policy literacy framework that goes beyond individual consent to address political-economic and infrastructural dimensions of surveillance.

title: Infrastructures of Surveillance and Control in the Invisible City of Waste
thesis: Surveillance technologies in Rotterdam's waste governance (oligopticons) engage in punitive politics that exceptionalize those who illegally dispose of waste, fighting difference rather than waste itself.
key_quotes: The epistemological move here is that this black boxing renders visible part of the urban ecology as data, without either explaining pollution events or providing an alternative to them. In other words, 'it is one thing to identify patterns; it is another to explain them. This requires social theory and deep contextual knowledge' (Kitchin 2014, 8) that are, however, not attended to. || Oligopticons of surveillance and control are producers of associations between practices of illegal waste disposal and abject nodes in the network, meaning notably those people living in poverty and other un-assignable exceptions to the scaffolding logic of 'modern' and 'participatory' urban life. || The oligopticon of surveillance and control works 'on people above all' (Latour and Hermant 2006, 55). The representation through oligopticons is part of the exception management that interweaves the materiality of waste in the city with people that are observed as exceptions to the modern way of life.
policy_relevance: Critiques punitive fines and surveillance as ineffective and harmful; suggests a more compassionate approach based on ethics of care and social/environmental justice, but does not offer specific policy recommendations.

title: The Banalisation of 'Suspicion': Politics of Prevention, Digitisation of Prediction, Fate of Travellers
thesis: Digitised predictive security based on a priori suspicion undermines democratic politics and criminal justice, banalising surveillance of all travellers.
key_quotes: The digitisation of data has accelerated this trend towards preventive security, which is created through the creation of specific data-organising categories according to algorithms, the sorting out of profiles of 'persons of concern' ranked according to their level of danger, and the so-called ability of artificial intelligence to predict the future behaviour of individuals in order to place some of them under surveillance. || It gives a 'magical' aura of scientific knowledge to dubious correlations and profoundly changes the way border controls are organised, creating categories of a priori suspicion that are applied to millions of people, and not just to so-called terrorists or radicalised individuals. || The databases of the European agency EU-LISA will help to show the functioning of this new 'dispositif' of suspicion, which endangers democratic politics.
policy_relevance: Discusses the EU AI Act's ban on individual predictive policing AI, the role of courts in limiting algorithmic suspicion, and the need for immediate action on high-risk AI regulation and suspension of data exchange agreements with the US.

title: Datafying citizens: Third-party trackers and data-as-payment in government infrastructure
thesis: Commercial third-party trackers on Scandinavian municipal websites impose hidden data costs on citizens, undermining the principle of universalism in welfare state governance.
key_quotes: The presence of tracking technologies thus amounts to an added cost of service that users pay when visiting websites, as their data is continuously collected and repurposed, including on government websites (Götze et al., 2022). || If an increased extraction of data can be equalled with increased cost, then the results suggest that this cost has increased over time in all three countries. || The embedded data infrastructures of Scandinavian municipal websites could thus be said to substantially undermine the principle of universalism, as they facilitate the market power of commercial, advertising-driven interests, Alphabet in particular.
policy_relevance: Recommends banning commercial tracking on municipal websites, removing advertising functions and analytical trackers like Google Analytics, switching to open-source technologies, and providing analogue alternatives for citizens who do not wish to be digitally included.

title: Policing the poor through space: The fil rouge from criminal cartography to geospatial predictive policing
thesis: Contemporary predictive policing perpetuates historical political and epistemic dictates linking crime to poverty and space, undermining the distinction between place-based and person-based predictions.
key_quotes: I argue that contemporary predictive mapping basically perpetuates the political and epistemic dictates which have historically framed the conceptualisation of crime in relation to space. || the application of algorithmic technologies to the domain of security is not in itself an epistemological break with past modalities. || the most visible discontinuities in the trajectory from the Cartographic school to the situational theories consist in the progressive dilution of the normative specificity of crime... Nevertheless, two major points ensure a fundamental epistemic continuity... First, the basic explanatory pattern is a rational action model uninterruptedly secured to the socio-economic deficit paradigm... Secondly, the aetiology of crime... is supported by a persisting ontologisation of crime which resorts to naturalistic metaphors.
policy_relevance: Calls for centering critique on the political meaning of crime predictability rather than technical fixes; no specific policy recommendations.

title: Making Crime Visible in the Digital Age: The Ethnomethods of Data Policing
thesis: Examines how police officers use ethnomethodological practices to interpret GPS location data, bridging interpretative gaps between decontextualized data and criminal activity.
key_quotes: The telephone data for us was useful because we knew that we were barking up at the right tree. Because with the telephone data we can see where people are going, we can see when people are sleeping, when they wake up, all this kind of information that are useful for us, and we could track his movement over a long-extended period of time. || It is commonly known that the police are expert in finding people and that they have developed an exquisite technology involving special facilities and procedures of sleuthing. It is less well appreciated that all this technology builds upon those socially structured features of everyday life that render persons findable in the first place (Bittner, 1967: 706; emphasis added). || The social world that the police deal with does not come pre-coded or neatly packaged and self-assigned as coming under the transgression of one particular law or type of incident. (Benson, 1993: 89).
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that data-driven policing requires interpretive work and that officers must balance suspicion with legal admissibility, implying policy should focus on transparency and accountability in data use, but no explicit recommendations are made.

title: Pre-Crime Prediction: does It Have Value? Is It Inherently Racist?
thesis: Predictive algorithms in policing have value but carry risks of bias, error, and infringement of rights; they should be used cautiously with human oversight.
key_quotes: O'Neil (2016, 2017), a mathematician and data scientist, insisted that algorithms were nothing more than opinions embedded in code. || Transparency was problematic because deep learning algorithms continually updated their pattern-finding function autonomously to reach the point where human programmers and/or analysts were unable to understand exactly how the final outcome was reached (i.e., the 'black-box conundrum') (O'Donnell, 2019, p. 546). || Lum and Isaac (2016) found PredPol dispatched police more often to minority neighborhoods and concluded that the PredPol algorithm tended to target Blacks at two times the rate of Whites. This disparate outcome was a consequence of a 'pernicious feedback loop' (O'Neil, 2016, p. 87).
policy_relevance: Recommends caution, transparency, accountability, and human rights protections; suggests using predictive tools for social services rather than purely punitive measures; notes need for long-term data collection (20 years) for policy assessment.

title: THE EFFECT OF BIG DATA ANALYTICS ON PREDICTIVE POLICING:THE MEDIATION ROLE OF CRISIS MANAGEMENT
thesis: Big data analytics significantly enhances predictive policing, with crisis management acting as a mediator in this relationship within Dubai police.
key_quotes: Predictive policing relies on computer algorithms to see patterns, predict the occurrence of future events based on large quantities of data, and aims to carefully target police presence to the necessary minimum to achieve desired results (Carrie and James, 2017, p.7). || Big data analytics is a process of collecting, aggregating, examining, and exploiting massive volumes of data from disparate and autonomous resources in order to identify patterns and other useful information for better managerial decisions (Sun, 2015). || The use of big data analytics provides excellent resources for achieving this goal, but is it enough to prevent or reduce the effect of crisis. Various studies have previously validated the use of big data analytics in policing, but with the mediation role of crisis management the performance of police will be enhance and can predict not only crimes but also crisis before it happens.
policy_relevance: The study recommends integrating big data analytics into police operations to enhance predictive policing and crisis management, with practical guidelines for UAE police forces. It also notes the need to balance technology use with privacy and ethical considerations.

title: Our Incriminating Lives
thesis: Dragnet surveillance through Palantir and ALPRs enables suspicionless, programmatic data collection that reifies racial inequality and expands police power beyond traditional criminal justice institutions.
key_quotes: The proliferation of digitized records makes it possible to merge data from previously separate institutional sources into an integrated, structural system... This integration facilitates one of the most transformative features of the big data landscape: the creep of criminal justice surveillance into other, non–criminal justice institutions. Function creep—the phenomenon of data originally collected for one purpose being used for another—contributes to a substantial increase in the data used by police. || Mass surveillance is not the 'natural' result of mass digitization. Instead, what we allow to proliferate and become the objects of massive data collection efforts are choices that reflect the social and political positions of the subjects and subject matter that we feel comfortable surveilling. || Digitized policing is different from traditional policing methods in a number of ways: the proliferation of automatic alert systems and shifts from query-based to alert-based systems makes it possible to systematically surveil ever larger groups of people; individuals with no direct police contact are now included in law enforcement systems, effectively lowering the threshold for inclusion in police databases; and institutional data systems are integrated, such that police now collect and use information gleaned from institutions that are typically not associated with crime control.
policy_relevance: Calls for resisting technological determinism; notes that mass surveillance is a political choice not an inevitability; implicitly argues for greater oversight and restrictions on data integration and function creep.

title: Directed Surveillance
thesis: Examines how predictive policing technologies in the LAPD create feedback loops of surveillance, reinforce social inequalities, and obscure bias through quantified risk scores.
key_quotes: Predictive policing simply refers to analytic techniques used by law enforcement to forecast potential criminal activity. || The point system may ultimately serve to prevent individuals already in the criminal justice system from being further drawn into the surveillance net, while obscuring the role of police practices in shaping risk scores. || By relying on data, rather than human interpretation, of crime patterns, one supervisor believed he could use predictive policing to allocate his resources more efficiently.
policy_relevance: Highlights how predictive policing can reinforce racial and spatial inequalities, and calls for scrutiny of algorithmic decision-making in policing. Notes legal compliance mechanisms and feedback loops that obscure bias.

title: Smart City Technologies: A Political Economy Introduction to Their Governance Challenges
thesis: Smart city technologies pose governance challenges related to inequality, discrimination, and surveillance, shaped by political economy factors like institutions, market, and ideology.
key_quotes: Smart city technologies ... can entrench inequality and discrimination patterns in cities’ fabric and turn cities into surveillance complexes. || The risk of enhancing surveillance through tools that are not meant for surveillance in the first place refers to the fact that even when certain digital technologies are not meant to surveil citizens, they may hold the capabilities to do so. || The chapter showed that even though digital technologies deployed in the city context hold the promise of making all sorts of processes, planning, and services more efficient, seamless, and quick, they can also entrench discrimination, inequality, and surveillance in a city’s fabric, and these effects cannot be easily displaced from the social and institutional contexts in which they operate.
policy_relevance: Discusses local surveillance ordinances, EU AI Act, and suggests political economy analysis can identify points of intervention for oversight and accountability.

title: Police Pushback: When the Watcher Becomes the Watched
thesis: Examines police officers' resistance to being surveilled by technologies repurposed from civilian surveillance, revealing power dynamics and function creep in big data policing.
key_quotes: Surveillance is fundamentally relational. The extent to which it is an exercise of power depends on the organizational contexts in which it is deployed, and how people feel about it depends on where they are in the organizational hierarchy. || Predictive algorithms are opaque, shrouded in 'algorithmic secrecy'. || The most vehement opposition was to function creep and quantified assessment when technologies and data originally designed for one purpose—such as risk management or crime reduction—were used for another, namely managerial assessment of job performance.
policy_relevance: Implications for transparency, data governance, and the need for clear metrics to evaluate data collection practices; highlights tensions between risk management and performance evaluation.

title: Coding Inequality: How the Use of Big Data Reduces, Obscures, and Amplifies Inequalities
geography: United States (Los Angeles, New York, Oakland)
thesis: Big data policing amplifies and obscures inequality through biased training data, feedback loops, secondary surveillance networks, and system avoidance, despite potential for accountability.
key_quotes: Rather than eliminating human discretion, big data is a form of capital, both a social product and a social resource. For that reason alone, big data cannot possibly obviate inequality: like other forms of capital, it is transactional, some people and groups have more of it than others, and it can be extracted from already disadvantaged populations. || Human judgment is hidden in the black box under a patina of objectivity. || When new technology is overlaid onto an old organizational structure, long-standing problems shape themselves to the contours of the new technology.
policy_relevance: Recommends transparency, community engagement, accountability from tech companies, ongoing validation of algorithms, and using big data to target services not just punishment.

title: The Public History and Private Future of Police Data
thesis: Traces the history of data-driven policing and argues that the current era is defined by unprecedented private sector involvement and military-to-police technology transfer.
key_quotes: He wanted, he said, to learn about technology to help 'catch bad guys in my city,' and the real innovations weren't being developed by law enforcement, but by tech startups and national defense. He'd come to DC to see whether there were any new counterinsurgency technologies that might be used in his department. || Tracing the corporate lineage of police surveillance technologies and the creep of military and corporate interests and practices into local law enforcement's daily operations is crucial for understanding the practice and institution of policing today. || The tendency for data or systems initially used for one purpose to be used for another, often unintended or unanticipated purpose, is known as 'function creep' and is a fundamental component of the big data landscape.
policy_relevance: Discusses implications of private sector involvement in policing, including reduced transparency and circumvention of privacy laws; notes that purchasing data from brokers can bypass constitutional protections.

title: Predict and Surveil: Data, Discretion, and the Future of Policing
thesis: Big data policing is fundamentally social, not objective, and its use in the LAPD amplifies inequality and displaces discretion to less visible parts of the process.
key_quotes: As I attended surveillance industry conferences and talked with individuals working in state, federal, and local law enforcement agencies, I learned that these agencies were starting to purchase licenses for analytic platforms originally designed for counterinsurgency efforts in Iraq and Afghanistan. One platform stood out early in my research—a platform designed by Palantir Technologies. || Private vendors can hide behind trade secrecy and nondisclosure agreements, ultimately circumventing typical public-sector transparency requirements and lowering the accountability of the police by making it harder for scholars to study, regulators to regulate, and activists to mobilize for or against specific practices. || The potential of big data is widely celebrated. Proponents argue it is more objective and can eliminate inequality by stripping discretion from biased front-line actors. But when we actually look at big data on the ground, we see that the use of big data does not replace discretion, but rather displaces discretionary power to earlier, less visible (and less accountable) parts of the policing process.
policy_relevance: Calls for curbing institutions' craving for data and offers guidelines for academics, lawmakers, and community groups to promote efficiency, fairness, and accountability in criminal justice reform (p. 16).

title: Decision
thesis: Algorithmic decisions are mundane, unexceptional partitions of abstract feature spaces based on calculations of distance, which produce and proliferate differences in urban governance.
key_quotes: Algorithms shape not only what we see, how we are taught, how books are written, how party manifestos are put together, but also what urban areas are policed, who is surveilled, and even who might be targeted by drones. || We propose to understand how heterogeneous algorithmic decisions are constitutive of another element of algorithmic reason and the government of difference. To do so, we 'follow' a predictive policing algorithm in order to unpack its decisions as distributed workflows and unexceptional data transformations. || PredPol had built on Pentagon funding for its co-founder Brantingham to develop a counterinsurgency model forecasting casualties in Iraq.
policy_relevance: Discusses accountability tools (principles, audits, certification, ethics boards) for algorithmic decision-making; critiques transparency as insufficient without infrastructure and expertise for effective use.

title: Making space with data: Data politics, statistics and urban governance in Denmark
thesis: Danish census data practices are central to spatialising and governing marginalised urban areas as 'ghettos', performing state authority and enabling top-down interventions.
key_quotes: In this article we engage with the contemporary data moment by exploring how particular data practices–– consisting of census data and statistics––have become embroiled in the making of urban space and governance in Denmark. || The use of census data by government to produce the ghetto list and by municipalities to monitor these areas performs an image of state, or municipal, vertical encompassment. || The data practices we have described are a crucial part of how the state, regions, and even local municipalities construct themselves as authorities over marginalised areas.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the use of census data for the ghetto list, which has consequences including forced displacement of residents through housing conversion policies. It highlights the need for accountability and the political nature of data practices in urban governance.

title: Caged by Data: Exposing the Politics of Facial Recognition Through Zach Blas’s Face Cages
thesis: Artistic interventions like Face Cages defamiliarize facial recognition to expose its violent reduction of identity and activate feminist critiques of biometric datafication.
key_quotes: The project exposes how biometric capta are not 'already out there' but rather need to be scanned and turned into digital code in order to be meaningful for the biometric apparatus. || Face Cages' violent aesthetic of the metal bars pressing into facial skin makes the violence implicit in biometric capta and capture visible and allows us to draw connections between current forms of biometric capture and the technologies' colonialist and racist histories. || Through the defamiliarizing image of the materialized biometric mask, Face Cages invites critical reflection on how we conceive of biometric data.
policy_relevance: None

title: Framing southern data-driven urban governance into data justice
thesis: Data-driven urban governance via Rio's 1746 CiRM system perpetuates socio-spatial injustices and fails to address structural inequalities, as revealed by a data justice framework.
key_quotes: data is not a neutral representation of reality but rather the product of a selective process that constructs particular versions of the world || the system has a limited capacity to democratize urban governance in Rio de Janeiro. While it facilitates the communication between citizens and the City Hall, it falls short in influencing long-term urban planning, fostering the inclusion of marginalized groups, and addressing underlying social structures. || the instrumentalization of data in Rio must be understood as part of an urban management culture, politically and symbolically embodied in the figure of Mayor Eduardo Paes, which prioritizes efficiency, the rationalization of public services, and results-oriented practices.
policy_relevance: The paper argues that data-driven urban governance systems must be evaluated through a data justice lens that addresses structural inequalities, not just efficiency. It calls for an integrated social justice agenda that connects data justice to struggles for urban reform and the right to the city, and warns against privatization and entrepreneurial urbanism.

title: Surveillance and violence from afar: The politics of drones and liminal security-scapes
geography: global (Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, US-Mexico border, US cities)
thesis: Drones as surveillance and military devices reveal violent articulations of US imperialism, dehumanization of targets, and the insidious application of militarized systems to domestic territories.
key_quotes: Within the current political and cultural milieu, this particular movement of military technology to civilian spheres reveals a symbiotic relationship between the war on crime and war on terror. || The drone stare is a type of surveillance that abstracts people from contexts, thereby reducing variation, difference, and noise that may impede action or introduce moral ambiguity. || In the case of drone surveillance in combat settings, the exclusionary politics of omniscient vision not only harm ethnic and cultural others with great prejudice, but they also instigate an additional violence of radically homogenizing local difference, lumping together innocent civilians with enemy combatants, women and children with wanted terrorist leaders.
policy_relevance: Warns against the erosion of civil liberties and the militarization of domestic spaces through drone surveillance; highlights the danger that existing legal protections and rights will be vitiated.

title: Qalandia Checkpoint as Space and Nonplace
thesis: Checkpoints in the Palestinian Territories function as both anthropological spaces and nonplaces, embodying Israeli control and Palestinian spatial fragmentation.
key_quotes: Nothing is transparent . . . it is never clear who will [pass] and who will not. . . . The reasons [for prohibiting Palestinians from passing] are so numerous, and the use made of them changes so much, that uncertainty becomes the ultimate system of control within the framework of the certainty of the occupation. || Checkpoints form part of the matrix of Israeli occupation, or if one prefers, colonialism and apartheid... which includes the wall/separation barrier... Israeli/settler-only access roads... policies of closures... and bureaucratic controls over Palestinian life. || Israel neither officially acknowledges legal responsibility for checkpoints nor recognizes them as 'sovereign' spaces. In this sense, checkpoints are constructed by the Israeli military not simply as a 'nonplace' but as 'bare space' that is part of a broader philosophical and political casting out of Palestinians as mere zoological humanity.
policy_relevance: None

title: Explaining spacio-cide in the Palestinian territory: Colonization, separation, and state of exception
geography: Palestinian territory (West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem)
thesis: The Israeli colonial project is 'spacio-cidal'—targeting land to induce 'voluntary' transfer of Palestinians—enabled by a regime of colonization, separation, and state of exception.
key_quotes: The Israeli settler-colonial project is not a genocidal project in a legal sense but a 'spacio-cidal' one. In every conflict, belligerents define their enemy and shape their mode of action accordingly. In the Palestinian–Israeli conflict, the Israeli target is the place. || The weapons of mass destruction are not so much tanks as bulldozers, which have destroyed streets, houses, cars, and dunam after dunam of olive trees. It is a war in an age of literal agoraphobia, the fear of space, seeking not the division of territory but its abolition. || Spacio-cide is mainly land confiscation in order to construct Jewish settlement, house demolition, and population transfer.
policy_relevance: Critiques the Oslo peace process and international community's reluctance to challenge Israeli settlement expansion; suggests that humanitarian organizations (e.g., UNRWA) inadvertently reinforce the state of exception by not advocating for refugee return.

title: THE LOCATION OF PALESTINE IN GLOBAL COUNTERINSURGENCIES
thesis: Palestine is a crucial node in the global transmission of counterinsurgency techniques, which are persistently used to control populations through spatial destruction and coercion.
key_quotes: This article concerns the horizontal circuits through which colonial policing or 'security' practices have been transmitted across time or from one location to another, with Palestine as either a point of origin or an intermediary node of transmission. || The use of hostages or human shields was suggested to the Palestine Police by A. F. Perrott of Peshawar: 'It might be worthwhile forming a "hostage corps" composed of the sons of hostiles. A couple of these in the front car of a convoy would discourage the use of landmines.' || Much of the old city of Jaffa was destroyed to punish Jaffan protests; this was done under the pretense of city planning and public hygiene and with twenty-four-hours' notice.
policy_relevance: None

title: Vertical Security in the Megacity: Legibility, Mobility and Aerial Politics
thesis: Megacity security is increasingly waged and consumed through the helicopter's machinic-prosthetic view, enabling legibility, mobility, and territorialization with violent consequences.
key_quotes: The article argues that megacity security marches to the rotator-beat of the police helicopter, fuelled by military technophilia (Graham, 2008) and in a context of the biopolitical desertion of the city’s most vulnerable. || By excavating the ambiguities of the helicopter’s machinic-prosthetic view, a perspective which may be distant and abstract, while also near and viscerally present, this article will explore how megacity security is increasingly waged and consumed. || In a way that Loïc Wacquant (2008) says is all but indistinguishable from military incursions into an occupied territory, megacity police forces such as Brazil’s policia militaria routinely intrude into shanty-towns with ‘blitzes’, during which low-flying helicopters knock off tin rooftops and troops break down doors and windows, ransack houses and bully their occupants, fire weapons indiscriminately, close down stores and schools, and carry out mass arrests for ‘vagrancy’.
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that permanent community policing, rather than temporary helicopter-based incursions, may be more effective, but also highlights the ambiguity of aerial security and the potential for helicopters to be used for terrorism.

title: The Occupation of the Senses: The Prosthetic and Aesthetic of State Terror
thesis: The settler colonial state uses sensory technologies (visual, auditory, olfactory) to manage and control the colonized population, producing racial exclusivity and spatial domination.
key_quotes: By 'occupation of the senses', I refer to technologies that manage language, sight, sound, time and space in the colony; the administration of who acts, who speaks, who gives birth and how, and who walks/moves/drives where and how; and what kind of language, music, smells, marches, colours, cultures and scenes are promoted and inscribed over the spaces, lives and bodies of the colonized. || Gil Hochberg (2015: 3) argues that an 'uneven distribution of "visual rights" undergirds the relationship between the Israeli occupier and the Palestinian occupied'. For Hochberg, '[h]ow much one can see, what one can see, and in what way one can see or be seen' are outcomes of socially constructed 'visual arrangements' produced and sustained by power relations || The marking of power by maiming a child's sight, produces and reproduces injustice by dispossessing the colonized of the space and also dispossessing the colonized body of its own senses.
policy_relevance: The paper calls for criminology to consider crimes against the senses and sensory deprivation as state crime, with implications for international law and human rights frameworks addressing settler colonial violence.

title: UNMANNING THE POLICE MANHUNT: VERTICAL SECURITY AS PACIFICATION
thesis: The repurposing of military drones for domestic policing reveals the continuity of war and police power under the logic of pacification, extending the manhunt as a foundational practice of police power.
key_quotes: military aerial drones are now being 'repurposed' as domestic security technologies || a number of our influential products have dual-use capability to locations and missions adjacent to our primary overseas ISR mission. One such example is local law enforcement, emergency first responders and border protection || the police drone is but one of the newest technologies that extends or reproduces the police's own design on the pacification of its territory
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the normalization of police drones and the security-accumulation assemblage, but does not offer explicit policy recommendations beyond a call to understand drones within the broader logic of pacification.

title: Driving while Palestinian in Israel and the West Bank: The politics of disorientation and the routes of a subaltern knowledge
thesis: Driving as a practice generates embodied political knowledge for Palestinians, revealing the politics of disorientation and fragmentation under Israeli rule.
key_quotes: Palestinian knowledge gained on the road is not disembodied and dispassionate... it resists expertise. || The road is not a neutral site of technical governance; it is a space of political hegemony and contestation. || Israel's management of the roads operates for Palestinians as a politics of disorientation, as routes change because of Israeli closure policies and as Palestinians encounter road signs and road infrastructure that subtly elide their presence.
policy_relevance: None explicitly; the paper implies the need to recognize subaltern knowledge and the political effects of infrastructure, but offers no direct policy recommendations.

title: Gated/gating community: the settlement complex in the West Bank
thesis: The Israeli settlement complex in the West Bank functions as a single gated/gating community that gates Palestinian space through a system of settlements, roads, and movement restrictions.
key_quotes: The argument of this paper, however, is different. The paper suggests that the settlement layout in the West Bank is not just an aggregate of 124 'legal' gated communities and a similar number of 'illegal outposts', but rather a single, contiguous gated community gating, in turn, Palestinian 'islands' within it. || The roads function as a barrier because its crossing is forbidden for Palestinians, and even approaching it is dangerous – be it for fear of harassment by soldiers or Border Patrol policemen, or for fear of the settlers who might be violent and unpredictable. || In the West Bank, self-gating and other-gating are one and the same.
policy_relevance: The paper suggests that the gated/gating community model, based on connectivity and exclusionarity, could be replicated elsewhere under perceived threat, with states enhancing connectivity for the privileged while reducing public space and freedom of movement for others.

title: Camps and Enclaves: Palestine in the Time of Closure
thesis: Refugee camps and enclaves in Palestine share a family resemblance as spatial devices for containing the displaced within a settler-colonial project, with enclaves representing a new form of inclusive exclusion through closure and immobility.
key_quotes: Enclaves here refer to territory surrounded by a state, where concentrated and confined populations, often culturally distinct and excluded from the state, are subject to its detailed regulations, which include severe restrictions on and close monitoring of place of residency and, most prominently, the scope and speed of mobility. || In 2006, when Dov Weisglass, an adviser to the then Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert, quipped in reference to the siege of Gaza that 'The idea is to put the Palestinians on a diet, but not to make them die of hunger'—a space opened for a critical discussion of bio-power. In enclaved Gaza, Israeli-imposed sanctions form a craftily spun web of restrictions that keeps Palestinian alive, just barely, on a highly restricted diet. || Without a publicly circulated plan to carve out and designate enclaves, they constitute legal and political grey zones with ambiguous borders in contrast to the more distinctly demarcated Bantustans, camps and reservations. This indeterminate grey zone makes life even more unbearable and ultimately more vulnerable.
policy_relevance: None

title: Border collapse and boundary maintenance: militarisation and the micro-geographies of violence in Israel–Palestine
thesis: Militarisation shapes micro-geographies of violence in Israel–Palestine through gendered dynamics of border collapse and boundary maintenance, sustaining occupation.
key_quotes: Drawing upon subaltern geopolitics and feminist geography, this article explores how militarisation shapes micro-geographies of violence and occupation in Israel–Palestine. || Here, the borders between homefront and battlefield break down at the same time as communal boundaries are reproduced, generating conditions of 'total militarism' wherein military interests and agendas are both actively and passively diffused. || As these individuals encounter the occupation in the spaces of everyday life they participate in militarisation, not passively but actively, taking up ambivalent positions that reveal more precisely how hegemonic power endures.
policy_relevance: None

title: Radical Indeterminancies: Affirmations and Subversions of the Separation Wall—The Case of the Palestinian Children of the Junction
thesis: Palestinian children crossing the Separation Wall simultaneously subvert and affirm Israel's performances of separation, revealing the border's epistemological and political functions.
key_quotes: The crux of my claim here is that these agents’ unique mobility punctuates and challenges Israel’s performances of separation (Jones 2012, 175). || The movements of these children allow us to detail the lived contours of what Eyal Weizman (2007) defines as 'The Hollow Land:' formal and informal spaces, paths and dimensions of passing, that appear and become prominent when and while spatial segregation is radicalized by the state of Israel. || When the child’s body is both a means to a political end, and still a child’s body, we—those who gaze at the child—know the child can no longer be a 'jahhil,' the traditional Palestinian image of a child as carefree and without any sort of political and economic consciousness.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the Israeli state's inaction regarding the Children of the Junction, noting that despite multiple Knesset sub-committee meetings, no practical steps were taken to care for the children. It highlights the bureaucratic and legal lacunae that prevent intervention.

title: Disrupting movements, synchronising schedules: Time as an infrastructure of control in East Jerusalem
thesis: Time operates as an infrastructure of control in East Jerusalem through two temporal regimes—deregulation (unpredictable) and synchronization (normalized)—that modulate Palestinian inclusion/exclusion and advance Israeli annexation.
key_quotes: Two temporal regimes are at work in Palestinian Jerusalem simultaneously. One deregulates time, making it unpredictable while causing time–space divergence. ... The other temporal regime, which I have called 'annexation time', normalises Palestinian schedules by synchronising the rhythms of urban mobility between East and West Jerusalem. || Time here functions as an immaterial infrastructure which tethers East Jerusalem to the West of the city and thereby perpetuates its annexation. || GPS devices were installed in the vehicles, allowing the monitoring of each bus’s whereabouts. While in the past, drivers frequently made detours... this was now no longer possible. The Operations Manager explained: 'We can see where he is, and we get an alarm if he goes off his route or is behind schedule.'
policy_relevance: Critiques Israeli policy of annexation through temporal control; shows how formalization of Palestinian transport reduces autonomy and normalizes occupation; time as adaptable infrastructure of control.

title: The Visibility of (In)security: The Aesthetics of Planning Urban Defences Against Terrorism
geography: UK, USA (London, Washington DC, New York)
thesis: Examines the paradox of visible vs. invisible counter-terrorism measures in urban spaces, showing how overt security can induce fear while invisible security risks uncontested surveillance.
key_quotes: security is becoming more civic, urban, domestic and personal: security is coming home (Coaffee & Murakami Wood, 2006: 504) || security features can arouse feelings of fear and anxiety by drawing attention to the fact that one’s safety and security is threatened (Boddy, 2007: 279) || invisible security, though potentially more aesthetically pleasing, and offering a redress to the many drawbacks of more obvious and obtrusive security interventions... must itself be treated with a healthy degree of scepticism
policy_relevance: Discusses the need for security features to be aesthetically acceptable and warns about the risk of invisible security leading to passive consent and uncontested expansion of surveillance.

title: How walls do work: Security barriers as devices of interruption and data capture
thesis: Security barriers are sociotechnical devices that govern populations through interruption and data capture, going beyond mere blockading.
key_quotes: I argue that understanding barriers as objects on their own stresses their blockading role, whereas employing an analytic of devices, where devices are thought to be productive, foregrounds what barriers work to produce. || The Falluja fence no longer exists, but the data it captured remains in use in Iraq and is still stored on servers in Virginia. || The massive aggregation of secret files on Iraqis, linked to permanent biometric identifiers, creates an unprecedented human rights risk that could easily be exploited by a future government.
policy_relevance: Highlights risks of biometric data aggregation and potential for misuse by future governments or non-state actors; cites concerns from EPIC, Privacy International, and Human Rights Watch.

title: Steel Walls and Picket Fences: Rematerializing the U.S.–Mexican Border in Ambos Nogales
thesis: The materialization of the US-Mexican border through Ambos Nogales emerges dialectically from fortification and transgression, shaping and being shaped by human agency.
key_quotes: The wall is the most visible and substantial instrument of the United States’ militarization of the Mexican border, but the wall has failed to secure the border. || The wall disrupts lives and breaks bodies. || The increasing militarization of the border with ever-growing delays to pass through the two downtown Nogales gates has led to a 30 percent decline in the number of people legally entering the United States between 2002 and 2011.
policy_relevance: The paper concludes that fortifying the border will not provide a viable solution to undocumented migration or drug smuggling, and that these issues cannot be addressed by building more walls.

title: Student Im/mobility in Birzeit, Palestine
thesis: Student mobilities in the West Bank are heavily impacted by Israeli occupation barriers, creating relative immobilities that shape experiences of home, place, and micropolitical responses.
key_quotes: Halper (2001, n.p.) uses the term 'Matrix of Control' to describe this state of affairs, a concept that is explicitly concerned with Palestinian immobility: 'The Matrix, an intricate and an interlocking series of control mechanisms, resembles the Japanese game of 'Go.' Instead of defeating your opponent as in chess, in 'Go' you win by immobilizing the other side, by gaining control of key points of a matrix, so that every time your opponent moves he or she encounters another obstacle.' || Weizman (2002) uses the phrase 'politics of verticality', to describe how three-dimensional space is crashed into six dimensions, three Jewish and three Arab... Rather, Weizman suggests the spatiality of occupation is 'Escher like', as Palestinians and Israeli spaces pass through, around, below and above one another: Israeli tunnels dive into Palestinians mountains; Palestinian dirt tracks pass beneath Israeli highways. || The immobilities students experience are relative not just to other peoples' mobility (e.g., Israeli settlers), but also to prior experiences of mobility (an 'else when') and to experiences of mobility in other spaces (an else where). Students experience the brute fact of their relative immobility through barriers that are material (checkpoints), legal-bureaucratic (the ID and permit system) and imaginative (e.g., Khader) in nature.
policy_relevance: The paper highlights the work of human rights organizations (B'Tselem), activist groups (Machsom Watch), and Birzeit University's 'Right to Education Campaign' that monitor and challenge movement restrictions. It also notes that high-level diplomatic negotiations frequently include demands to reduce barriers to movement.

title: A Cartography of the Unknowable: Technology, Territory and Subterranean Agencies in Israel’s Management of the Gaza Tunnels
thesis: The subterranean materiality of Gaza tunnels frustrates Israel's techno-scientific efforts to know and secure territory, destabilizing state sovereignty and risk management.
key_quotes: the tunnels are perceived as a serious threat by Israel’s strategic decision-makers because they are a technology of occlusion that makes use of the material properties of the earth to subvert the Israeli state’s apparatuses of surveillance and calculation to secure against danger. || the soil’s ability to obfuscate techniques through which data can be gathered, analysed and used to predict future threats profoundly alters the calculus through which the political logic of risk operates in a fundamental way. || This dual-use arrangement has made the tunnels a crucial infrastructure in maintaining Hamas’ viability as the political hegemon inside Gaza, both financially as a source of income to sustain its government, and militarily as a logistical conduit.
policy_relevance: The paper references the Israeli State Comptroller's report criticizing political leadership for failing to act on tunnel intelligence, implying a need for better integration of intelligence and technology, but offers no explicit policy recommendations.

title: Israel's Biospatial Politics: Territory, Demography, and Effective Control
geography: Israel/Palestine (including West Bank, East Jerusalem, Negev, Galilee)
thesis: Israel's colonial project uses biospatial strategies—demographic classifications and land dispossession—to racialize space and maintain effective control over territory between the Jordan Valley and the Mediterranean.
key_quotes: The term biospatial denotes the deployment of such biotechniques to demarcate, control, manage, shape, and ascribe signification to space. || The algorithm developed by the CBS to distinguish between these two groups is based in part on where they live, namely, in a 'Jewish locality' or a 'non-Jewish' one. This suggests that race and space are mutually constitutive; biotechniques are used to produce a population's racial (and other) identity and in this way to racialize the inhabited space, while space itself helps determine the population's identity. || The CBS does not include these Bedouin villages in the count of localities and asks the people inhabiting them to indicate the name of their tribe instead of an address, thus revealing, yet again, the CBS's power of interpellation while severing the bio from space.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the 'good Israel/bad Israel' framing and argues that Israel's biospatial policies produce a single apartheid state. It implies that international support for Israel as a democracy is complicit in these policies.

title: Drone Use for COVID-19 Related Problems: Techno-solutionism and its Societal Implications
thesis: The pandemic-driven use of drones by authorities creates a new socio-technical assemblage that accelerates regulatory processes, normalizes exceptionalism, and expands surveillance, with limited public contestation.
key_quotes: Equipping drones with spraying functions is not a new attribute, as the technology has been used in a similar way for spraying pesticides at agricultural sites. Yet the objective of these spraying drones, namely, to disinfect public areas to avoid the spread of a virus, is an example of function expansion to face a new problem. || The recent drone use by national authorities has largely taken place without widespread contestation, unlike the public criticism we have seen towards contact tracing apps, which itself has led local and national governments to revert or revise decisions on these apps. || C-UAS technology is a surveillance system, which raises privacy concerns and can lead to psychological stress and to elevation of threat perception. It is part of a growing militarization of law enforcement and often takes civilian-military entanglements a step further.
policy_relevance: The paper provides policy implications: accelerate regulation without reducing safety/privacy, continuously review ethical/legal implications of drone technology, involve public and civil society in regulation, and debate social/political impacts of technology.

title: URBAN WARFARE ECOLOGY: A Study of Water Supply in Basrah
thesis: Protracted armed conflict and sanctions degrade urban water services through cumulative direct, indirect, and brain-drain impacts, requiring a shift from relief-rehabilitation-development models to sustained support within urban warfare biospheres.
key_quotes: 'Dual-use' restrictions are particularly problematic for restoring water services. The impact in Gaza of the Israeli denial of a vast range of material deemed to serve military as well as civilian purposes is well-known to those agencies attempting emergency and development efforts there. || The analysis attributes a step-wise decline in service quality to a lack of water treatment chemicals, a lack of spare parts, and, primarily, an extended 'brain-drain' of qualified water service staff. || The urban warfare ecology lens is found to be a useful complement to 'infrastructural warfare' research, suggesting the study of protracted armed conflict upon all aspects of urban life be both deepened technically and broadened to other cases.
policy_relevance: Calls for longer-term, flexible funding models and sustained technical support to local water operators, moving beyond the relief-rehabilitation-development (RRD) paradigm in chronic urban conflict settings.

title: Performing colonial sovereignty and the Israeli ‘separation’ wall
thesis: The Israeli separation wall performs colonial sovereignty by constructing a psychic border between civilized inside and uncivilized outside while also revealing internal contestations within the Israeli state.
key_quotes: The wall by no means represents a simple division of territory: it does not run along the 1967 borders (the 1949 Armistice line) that are internationally agreed upon as the basis for future peace settlement, and in fact, at 708 kilometres, the wall is more than double the length of the 'Green Line'. || As a performance of sovereignty, the way in which it encloses and 'blocks off' Palestinian presence can be read as immensely powerful. To 'disappear' the other, to create the demography desired is the ultimate expression of (bio-)sovereignty in the ethnic-exclusive state. || The wall both veils and partially constitutes 'the violent reality of a shifting colonial frontier' (Weizman, 2007, p. 179), and the 'us here'/'them there' ideology it supposedly performs is undermined by the settlement enterprise.
policy_relevance: Critiques the wall's security discourse and separation ideology, arguing that it inhibits productive encounters and undermines Palestinian security; suggests a need to shift towards coexistence.

title: Checkpoint Knowledge: Navigating the Tunnels and Al Walaja Checkpoints in the Occupied Palestinian Territories
thesis: Checkpoints are spatial political technologies that produce two mobility regimes—smooth for Jewish settlers and controlled for Palestinians—through low-tech design and arbitrary biopolitical categorization, which Palestinians navigate using 'checkpoint knowledge'.
key_quotes: As stated by Yael Berda (2018), the occupation regime should not be seen as a regime of rights but rather as a 'regime of privileges'. She explained that the Palestinian subject is dependent upon the goodwill of the ruler. || The decision of who is stopped and who can pass unhindered is thus made solely by the soldiers. || Palestinian commuters used various tactics based on their 'checkpoint knowledge' to try to make their passages as smooth as possible.
policy_relevance: None explicitly, but the paper highlights the arbitrary and humiliating nature of checkpoints, implicitly calling for recognition of human rights violations.

title: (Non)-lethality and war: tear gas as a weapon of governmental intervention
thesis: Tear gas is examined as a technology of governmentality, tracing its history from colonial to contemporary uses to reveal continuities in liberal power and the blurring of war and peace.
key_quotes: In examining the history of tear gas, I argue that this technology has been complicit in the demarcation of this frontier and continues to participate in its delineation in the contemporary moment. || As Sloterdijk suggests, 'When the body of the enemy can no longer be liquidated with direct assault, the possibility presents itself to the attacker of making his existence impossible, by immersing the enemy in an unlivable milieu.' || The 'weaponization' – to use the words of the report – of tear gas as a tool of general repression, terrorising activists by launching tear gas at any time of day or night into their homes, is a manifestly different type of use that betrays a bellicose logic with the tools of domestic governance.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques the normalisation of tear gas and calls for reflection on its use as a tool of governance that blurs war and peace, with implications for international law and policing.

title: Kafka at the West Bank checkpoint: de-normalizing the Palestinian encounter before the law
thesis: Alternative filmic representations of the West Bank checkpoint de-normalize the encounter, revealing it as a manifestation of Agamben's state of exception and sovereign law.
key_quotes: the checkpoint has emerged as a quintessential trope within the contemporary Palestinian imagination, to such an extent that 'checkpoint narratives' have arguably come to assume a dangerously 'normalized' status as everyday, even iconic features of Palestinian existence. || the article argues that apprehension of the enduring oddity and abnormality of the checkpoint serves as a vital mode of critical resistance to the policies of 'spatio-cide' 'securitization' and colonialism exercised at the hands of the State of Israel through the checkpoint mechanism. || the checkpoint operates as a physical manifestation of the 'state of exception' exercised by Israel as 'sovereign law', according to which the Palestinian subject is reduced to the status of 'homo sacer'
policy_relevance: Suggests that de-normalization of checkpoint narratives is a form of resistance; references BDS movement in notes.

title: Arrested in Place: Palestinian Children and Families at the Border
geography: occupied Palestinian territories (West Bank, Gaza, East Jerusalem)
thesis: Explores how Palestinian children and families experience visible and invisible borders under Israeli occupation, revealing how these borders restrict movement and arrest them in place, while also demonstrating resilience and resistance.
key_quotes: These policies contribute to what Halper (2000) has termed Israel's ‘matrix of control’, which is the practice of cultivating artificial borders, limiting movement within and across borders, and effectively suppressing everyday life within the oPt. || the ‘hollowing’ of Palestinian land (Weizman, 2007) creates new facts on the ground that mark Israel’s presence and re-signifies Palestinian territory as belonging to Israel. || Abu-Majd remarked: ‘Our children are used to living like anyone who is in prison. You see our house is covered with these bars?’
policy_relevance: None

title: The security-threat-community
thesis: Examines how Troubles-era social-housing redevelopment in Belfast became an instrument of security policy, creating the 'security-threat-community' where housing need was subordinated to military threat assessment.
key_quotes: The paper makes visible the sophisticated socio-material effects of these operations and illustrates how they remain embedded within contemporary community structures. The paper concludes by reflecting on how this permits conflict-era forces to remain active, but largely unacknowledged, within the post-conflict era.
policy_relevance: Argues for a 'revaluing of the value' of conflict-architecture within post-conflict policy frameworks, noting that the Together: Building a United Community Strategy fails to recognise the security-threat-community as a legacy of conflict. Recommends cross-departmental political process to address the hidden spatial divisions.

title: Non-state space: the strategic ejection of dangerous and high maintenance urban space
thesis: The paper introduces the concept of 'autotomic space' to describe how state, policing, and citizen strategies strategically eject dangerous or high-maintenance urban spaces to minimize costs and maintain the integrity of the remaining city.
key_quotes: autotomic in nature – spaces that are ejected in order to avoid losses or further damage to the body politic of the city in ways akin to the response of certain animals that protect themselves from predation by shedding a limb or body part. || we have sought to develop understandings of public space and city/neighbourhood governance using this metaphor of ejection as a kind of strategic reflex action by threatened governments, citizens and private service providers. || The no-go area thus exemplifies not only resistance to authority as is commonly understood, but also the deployment of a kind of power that stems from disregard.
policy_relevance: The paper critiques autotomic strategies as deepening inequality and spatial injustice but does not offer explicit policy recommendations; it calls for recognizing the paradoxical nature of control through abandonment.

title: Crafting and reinforcing the state through security privatisation: territorialisation as a public–private state project in East Jerusalem
thesis: Security privatisation can reinforce state territorialisation by enabling unequal protection and evading accountability, as shown in Jewish-Israeli settlement compounds in East Jerusalem.
key_quotes: In this article, I seek to extend our understanding of the state’s changing role in policing and the enmeshing of state and non-state security actors through an exploration of the new public–private security configurations around East Jerusalem’s settlement compounds. || I suggest that the governmental policy of encompassing East Jerusalem into the state’s fold, despite legal, diplomatic and public opinion limitations, was pursued through a solution found on the private market. || Weizman (2007) explored how different forms of Israeli rule inscribe themselves in space, positing that the Israeli architecture in Jerusalem simultaneously embodied and rejected the old Palestinian cityscape (2007, p.43–44). Likewise, the sight of Jewish-Israeli settlement compounds – Palestinian houses transformed into urban fortresses and topped by towering flags – mirrors the ambivalence towards the indigenous Palestinian design and its competition with the thrust towards modernity and distinguishability.
policy_relevance: The paper argues that security privatisation allows states to evade accountability and deflect legal challenges, with implications for human rights and democratic governance. It highlights the need for greater transparency and accountability in public-private security arrangements.

title: Necronationalism: managing race, death and the nation's skeletons
thesis: Settler colonial nation-building in Israel/Palestine operates through the management of dead Indigenous bodies, a practice termed 'necronationalism' that extends necropower beyond life to govern the conditions of life after death.
key_quotes: The capacity to govern life after death is still firmly rooted in the reach of colonial power, and that by attending to the excavation and erasure of Mamilla Cemetery's deceased Palestinian subjects, we see a particular configuration of sovereignty defined through a calculus of absence. || Necronationalism signals attention to practices of settler colonial nation-building organized around the colonial management of dead racial (Indigenous) subjects through the strategic displacement of their corporeality. || What we see emerging in this particular instance of necronationalism is a practice of national memory formation built upon the management of death and its artifacts.
policy_relevance: None

title: No Way Through: approaching the West Bank checkpoint
thesis: Examines how cultural narratives use proxy crossings at the West Bank checkpoint to generate empathy and solidarity with Palestinians, while also exposing the limits of substitution.
key_quotes: This highly visible instance of the global checkpoint is the site of a spectacular confrontation between opposing notions of safety, embodied in the encounter between the Israeli soldier guarding the checkpoint and the Palestinian who seeks to pass through it. || the occupation's matrix of concrete and control; the settlements, the roads, the 'terminals', and the Wall going up were like a net thrown out over the hills and valleys of the West Bank, and the Palestinian areas choked in between. || The checkpoint thus becomes a site of political conversion, a site where the protagonist, standing in for the reader or viewer, can be persuaded to stand in solidarity with Palestinians.
policy_relevance: None explicitly; implies cultural advocacy can influence public opinion on the occupation.

title: Negotiating Boundaries, Narrating Checkpoints: The Case of Machsom Watch
thesis: Analyzes how Machsom Watch activists challenge Israeli territorial policies by observing, documenting, and personalizing checkpoints to reframe security and morality.
key_quotes: In contrast to the open violence, the occupying forces also engage in hidden violence. There is bureaucratic violence, which the film attached to this report attempts to uncover. || The politicization of the Holocaust as a constituting factor in Israeli national identity, and in justifying any and all action as necessary defensive measures, is contested by Watchers’ activism ... Remembering the silence of the majority during the Nazi/fascist period impels many of us to speak out, now, while there is still time. || Just imagine the amount of time you are wasting over the last four years. Even if you are crossing [the checkpoint] and people [soldiers] are polite, just try to calculate how much time is being wasted. People are late to their job if they are lucky enough to have one. People cannot really study, work or live because every inch of their autonomy is being controlled by someone else.
policy_relevance: Highlights activism that challenges occupation policies and documents human rights abuses; notes tensions between humanitarian improvements and legitimating the checkpoint regime.

title: Folding and Enfolding Walls: Statist Imperatives and Bureaucratic Aesthetics in Divided Jerusalem
thesis: The paper analyzes a vector of wall-like architectural forms in Jerusalem as a topological mechanism of statist control, folding and enfolding space to reinforce state imperatives and destroy Palestinian urban life.
key_quotes: The effect of the security barrier will be to destroy Palestinian metropolitan Jerusalem 'and control it without annexing it' (Klein 2005: 71). || Up close, it is a row of huge blunt teeth sunk into the earth, their bite savage and unyielding. Horizons of living are blocked, perspective severely foreshortened. One cannot look over, under, or around. || Beginning with the harmonic pylon-parabola as the entry to the historic and holy capital, gathering sacrificial empowerment through the museum-wall, its velocity becoming more directional, the vector accelerates through the mall-wall, gathering the power to own and fetishize, pinning Palestinians-as-objects against the security barrier with Holocaust history, squeezing, flattening, and sacrificing them with the power to consume against its unyielding, brute form.
policy_relevance: None. The paper critiques existing state practices but does not offer policy recommendations.

title: Imagining the Biometric Future: Debates Over National Biometric Identification in Israel
thesis: Both proponents and opponents of Israel's national biometric identification system used competing sociotechnical imaginaries of security to shape the system's legislative and technological outcomes.
key_quotes: Usually, security is offered as a justification for biometric identification. In the Israeli debate, security was foundational to both claims for and against the system. || Security, and the belief that technological innovations can enhance it, have long been priorities in the Israeli polity and ground collectively held visions of desirable futures. || By generating a dialectic of sociotechnical imaginaries animated by already well-established collective aspirations for security, opponents and proponents contested the very meaning of security itself by defining it, and its relationship to biometric technologies, in different ways.
policy_relevance: The paper shows that sociotechnical imaginaries can shape the legislative and technological design of national surveillance systems, leading to compromises that incorporate both security and privacy concerns (e.g., the database was kept but with reduced data).

title: Security Assemblages and Spaces of Exception: The Production of (Para)Militarized Spaces in the U.S. War on Drugs
thesis: The war on drugs paramilitarizes space through security assemblages that blur policing and war, producing spaces of exception for illiberal governance.
key_quotes: Security centres around the management of flows of people and resources by means of configuring and re-configuring space. || The hyperghetto and the prison are instruments for controlling risky populations. But they also constitute risky spaces that, due to the very fact that they warehouse risky populations, need to be constantly monitored, controlled, policed and targeted by a variety of different tactics and technologies. || The war on drugs has eroded the very boundaries between policing and war-fighting, it has also led to what we may call the 'policization' of the military.
policy_relevance: Critique of war on drugs and paramilitarization; implications for understanding security assemblages and spaces of exception.

title: Colonialist Construction in the Urban Space of Jerusalem
thesis: Israel uses territorial and demographic engineering in Jerusalem to construct a Zionist identity-based space, while Palestinians resist through various practices.
key_quotes: Israel employs various methods in this identity-based urban project. Archaeology and territorial reconfiguration become means for constructing the Israeli subject and society, while simultaneously deconstructing the Palestinian equivalents. || In 2011, 622 Palestinian structures were demolished by Israeli authorities in the Occupied Territories, resulting in the displacement of 1,094 people. || The Wall’s noncontiguity, nonlinearity, porosity, shifting evolution, and enclosures of settler populations are a deterritorialization of space.
policy_relevance: The paper implies that international law and human rights frameworks are insufficient to counter Israeli practices; it highlights the need for accountability and recognition of Palestinian sovereignty.

title: Geometry after the Circle: Security Interventions in the Urban Gray Zone
thesis: The paper argues that despite fantasies of post-geometric urban warfare, security interventions in African urban gray zones inevitably resort to the circle (cordon sanitaire), and outsourcing to surrogate forces does not overcome this basic geometry.
key_quotes: The West Point cordon sanitaire was, by any measure, a disaster. Soldiers and police officers responded to rioting West Point residents with beatings and with shots fired, wounding a teenage boy who bled to death before he could receive medical care. || The combination of urban chaos and the deployment of the armed forces of the Liberian state turned a health emergency into an act of urban war. || What is new about the current moment of militarization across Africa and around the globe is not its kinetic formations. It is the way the discourses and fantasies of contemporary urban space and urban threats render familiar formations largely invisible.
policy_relevance: None

title: The Common Camp: Temporary Settlements as a Spatio-political Instrument in Israel-Palestine
thesis: The camp is a versatile spatio-political mechanism used for territorial expansion and exclusion in Israel-Palestine, functioning beyond Agamben's 'space of exception' to include both control and resistance.
key_quotes: Camps are extensively employed by both authoritarian regimes and contemporary democracies as instruments of control, custody, care and abandonment. || This new conceptualization of the camp allows it to be examined as a complex territorial instrument which belongs to the variety of radical spatio-political practices. || They push you into a corner. While being deprived of any “life supporting” mechanisms such as economic resources, infrastructures or state services, the residents of Rachme are at the same time exposed to direct state violence and being controlled by tight surveillance.
policy_relevance: Implications for spatial planning, recognition of Bedouin villages, and understanding the political use of temporary settlements as tools of displacement.

title: Architecture as event space: Violence, securitisation, and resistance
geography: global, with focus on Israel/Palestine, US, UK, China
thesis: Architecture is an active political agent in security practices and resistance, analyzed through Tschumi's event space concept and Weizman's forensic architecture.
key_quotes: 'There is no architecture without action, no architecture without events, no architecture without program … no architecture without violence.' (Tschumi, quoted p. 368) || 'buildings are not static entities … they continually undergo dynamic transformations' (Weizman, quoted p. 370) || 'the architecture of occupation … [is met with] a counter architecture, which involves (among other things) redesigns that create possibilities of mobility that the Separation Wall and checkpoints stymie.' (p. 382)
policy_relevance: Implicitly calls for forensic architecture as a critical practice to document war crimes and human rights violations in urban contexts.

title: Bible and Gun: Militarism in Jerusalem’s Holy Places
thesis: Religious militarism is embedded in the physical construction and use of Jerusalem's holy sites, promoting violence and sacrifice in the name of national religious ideology.
key_quotes: Within days after the 1967 War, the Israeli authorities demolished the Palestinian Magharib Quarter that stood in front of the Wall in order to create the large open plaza that stands there today and accommodates large numbers of people who flock there, including the pious, tourists, and the merely curious. || Today, the Tomb is completely enveloped by the concrete separation barrier making it available to Israeli Jews and tourists coming from Jerusalem in approved vehicles, but inaccessible to Palestinians. It has become a military zone, literally an urban fortress. || The extreme conditions of Rachel’s Tomb require further description. The sense of isolation, fortification and religiosity begins in the centre of Jerusalem.
policy_relevance: The paper highlights how religious militarism at holy sites reinforces an embattled city and undermines viability for all inhabitants, implying the need to address occupation and dispossession, but offers no explicit policy recommendations.

title: Walled in/walled out in the West Bank: performing separation walls in Hany Abu-Assad's Omar
thesis: Analyzes the representation of the West Bank wall in Hany Abu-Assad's film Omar as both a physical reality of the state of exception and a site of radical potentiality.
key_quotes: 'At the core of this military urbanism lies the mechanism of walling. In particular, the wall that makes up the West Bank security barrier, erected in 2002 by the Israeli Government ostensibly to protect Israeli civilians from Palestinian militant attacks, constitutes the strongest spatial manifestation of an unyielding state of exception – the place where life has lost its political existence.' (p.124) || 'Omar's vertical performance of the wall relates to the concept of 'the politics of verticality' developed by Weizman (2002, 2003, 2007; Segal and Weizman 2003) to grasp the three-dimensionality of the architecture of occupation in the West Bank.' (p.128) || 'The wall is presented in Omar as the ultimate visual expression of dominion, a dynamic that plays itself out continually in a context of asymmetrical power dynamics, of an unequal access to visual rights (Hochberg 2015).' (p.129)
policy_relevance: None

title: The changing character of Israel's occupation: planning and civilian control
thesis: Israel uses planning and land policy instruments in the West Bank to restrict Palestinian development and enable settlement expansion, continuing occupation through bureaucratic means.
key_quotes: The plan emphasised that insofar as areas adjacent to the 1948/49 armistice Green Line were concerned, 'immediate action on the subject of planning is essential both within and outside the area' (WZO, 1983, 7–8). || Israel has made use of the power to demolish houses with increased vigilance over the past decade (Bimkom, 2008). In fact, a recent report notes that in June 2009, OCHA recorded the single highest monthly total of Area C demolitions since it developed its database, in 2005. || as the percentage of rejections increases, Palestinians lose hope that they will succeed in obtaining one, and apply for permits only as a stop-gap measure when demolition orders to existing structures have been published.
policy_relevance: Describes how planning and land policy under occupation violate international law and humanitarian principles, with implications for peace negotiations and the two-state solution. The paper calls for planners to recognize ethical duties to all affected populations.

title: Bear Witness: Embedded Coverage of Turkey's Urban Warfare and the Demarcation of Sovereignty against a Dynamic Exterior
thesis: Analyzes how state television series 'Bear Witness' uses embedded reporting to portray urban warfare as a dynamic exterior threatening sovereignty, while fostering viewer identification with law enforcement.
key_quotes: In his work on the Israeli military's operations in Palestinian neighborhoods and towns, Eyal Weizman has interpreted the destruction of homes as a shift in the object of the state's pursuit of strengthening its sovereignty through siege warfare. The shift is from the walls of another state to those of the home. || The effect of the recent and ongoing curfews across the region has been to altogether evacuate curfew-affected areas rather than just oblige residents to stay indoors, thus sealing entire neighborhoods off from the outside world. || Bear Witness detaches the state and its claim to sovereignty from the places and times in which the operations are carried out. These places and times are thus rendered the spatiotemporal exterior of sovereignty.
policy_relevance: None. The paper analyzes propaganda and sovereignty but does not offer policy recommendations.

From SARS to COVID-19: Digital infrastructures of surveillance and segregation in exceptional times
thesis: Compares digital surveillance and segregation measures during SARS and COVID-19 in three jurisdictions, arguing that temporary crisis infrastructures can have long-term effects on state power and are shaped by sociopolitical contexts.
key_quotes: However, even after the precipitating crisis fades, the surveillance and segregating infrastructures built to respond to the initial threats can remain permanent. || The individualized nature of ‘mobile quarantines’ however makes it far harder to pinpoint the contours of segregation, compared to more traditional quarantine orders. || In China, the technical capabilities developed to generate and deploy individual-based quarantine orders in the form of health codes has fundamentally transformed the way segregation is and may continue to be administered.
policy_relevance: Warns that temporary digital infrastructures can become permanent and that governments should consider long-term effects on privacy, trust, and civil liberties; notes that the extent of surveillance depends on sociopolitical context and calls for caution regarding mission creep.

title: Is civic data governance the key to democratic smart cities? The role of the urban data trust in Sidewalk Toronto
thesis: Sidewalk Labs' Urban Data Trust was designed to assetize residents' data and entrench rentiership, showing how even civic data governance can be corrupted by platform capitalism.
key_quotes: I present the story of the Urban Data Trust as a cautionary tale. It demonstrates that even civic projects are not immune to a rentiership economy when they seek to profit from data. || the real purpose of the Urban Data Trust was to assetize residents’ information and make it sufficiently easier for technology companies to access, reuse, and profit from the data. || the trust was designed to extract value from the smart city data by making it easier for private actors to collect, reuse, and monetize it.
policy_relevance: Discusses policy implications of data assetization and rentiership, referencing GDPR, CCPA, and Canadian Digital Charter. Suggests that treating data as an asset can corrupt civic initiatives, but offers no specific policy recommendations.

title: The effect of spatiotemporal resolution on predictive policing model performance
thesis: Evaluates how varying grid resolution, temporal resolution, and historical time frame affect predictive policing model performance to identify optimal parameter values.
policy_relevance: None explicitly, but discusses implications for police resource allocation and the trade-off between prediction performance and spatiotemporal resolution.
